title: UPDATE 2-Danish bonds rally as  FX interventions  stoke rate cut talk
text:
(Updates with analyst comment, context)

By Dhara Ranasinghe

LONDON, Jan 5 (Reuters) - Denmark's short-dated borrowing costs fell on Wednesday, as news of heavy currency market interventions to weaken the Danish crown stoked speculation that the central bank would soon resort to an interest rate cut.

According to data released on Tuesday, Denmark's central bank last month sold 47 billion Danish crowns, worth more than $7 billion, to defend its currency's peg against the euro.

While it has been selling crowns to stabilise its strengthening currency since March 2021, December marked the biggest monthly intervention since early 2020.

Those purchases have taken Denmark's foreign exchange reserves to the highest since 2015, at almost 530 billion Danish crowns ($81 bln).

But economists reckon authorities may have to follow up those interventions by cutting interest rates.

Denmark's central bank does not have regular monetary policy meetings but the board of governors convenes whenever necessary. It usually announces rate decisions on a Thursday at 5pm local time.

Another cut soon would follow a September move, which came after months of currency interventions failed to sufficiently weaken the crown.

The Danish central bank's sole mandate is to maintain the peg and keep the crown within a band of 7.29252 to 7.62824 crowns per euro.

The rate cut speculation, is now playing out in bond markets where yields fell sharply, suggesting investors are starting to position for such a move.

The yield on Denmark's three-year bond was down almost 7 basis points (bps) on Wednesday at -0.50%.

Five-year bond yields were down 3 bps at -0.34%.

"They have shown a long-standing willingness to defend the exchange rate peg and that won't change anytime soon," said David Oxley, a senior European economist at Capital Economics, referring to Danish central bank policy makers.

"In September, the rate cut was a logical solution to the upward pressure on the peg so if the crown is under pressure again that they will do what it takes to maintain the peg."

While money market futures so far suggest only a 20% chance of a 10 bps rate cut in February, speculation is building.

Nordea analysts said another rate cut could be imminent while Soren Kristensen, chief economist at Sydbank, saw a possible 10-15 bps move during the first quarter.

Oxley at Capital Economics said Denmark could cut rates to as low as -0.75% without opening up too much of a gap with the European Central Bank's key rate at -0.50%.

At -0.60%, the key Danish interest rate is already among the lowest in the world and a rate cut would contrast with policy in most other developed economies, where central banks are scaling back stimulus and lifting borrowing costs from ultra-low levels as inflation picks up.

Not all see a rate cut as a done deal. Danske Bank noted upward crown pressure was now receding, meaning currency interventions might be considered sufficient.

Claus Hvidegaard, head of fixed income research Denmark, at SEB, says higher currency intervention were more of a reflection of the central bank's wish to boost excess liquidity, and keep money market rates stable versus the euro area.

"We see it as much more of a liquidity exercise, so we think they will have to intervene more in currency markets to boost liquidity before they consider another rate cut."

(Reporting by Dhara Ranasinghe in London and Nikolaj Skydsgaard in Copenhagen; Editing by Sujata Rao, Mark Potter and Hugh Lawson)

title: UPDATE 1-Danish  FX  reserves shrink after large  central bank intervention
text:
(Adds analyst comments, background)

COPENHAGEN, Jan 3 (Reuters) - Denmark's foreign exchange reserves fell by more than 4 billion crowns in December after the central bank made its largest intervention in the currency market in three months, it said on Friday.

"We need to go back four years, since there has been an intervention three months in a row, and the central bank is potentially not done," chief economist at Arbejdernes Landsbank, Jeppe Borre, said in a note.

Denmark's foreign exchange reserves fell to 435.4 billion crowns ($65.05 billion) in December from 440.7 billion crowns at the end of November, the central bank said.

It bought 4.1 billion crowns in December to keep the currency stable against the euro, to which it is pegged, it said.

In October and November, the central bank only bought 0.4 and 1.2 billion crowns respectively.

Since the central bank cut its key rate to its lowest level ever in September, mirroring a cut by the ECB, the crown has steadily weakened to levels not seen since 2015.

In 2015, the Danish central bankintervened heavily to stave off foreign investors buying crowns in the hopes that Denmark would abandon its fixed peg to the euro.

"The central bank's rate cut has, all things being equal, been more significant than that of the ECB, which contributes to the weakening of the crown," chief economist at Arbejdernes Landsbank, Jeppe Borre, said in a note.

($1 = 6.6934 Danish crowns) (Reporting by Nikolaj Skydsgaard; Editing by Kirsten Donovan and Nick Macfie)

title: *S&PGR Affirms Denmark 'AAA/A-1+' Ratings; Outlook Stable
text:
8 Mar 2019 16:12 ET  Press Release: S&PGR Affirms Denmark 'AAA/A-1+' Ratings; Outlook Stable


 
 
The following is a press release from S&P Global Ratings: 
 
OVERVIEW 
     -- Denmark's economy is in a strong position, in our view, and will 
continue to grow by 1.7% over the coming years, despite slower global trade 
and a reduction in households' ratio of debt to disposable income. 
     -- Denmark continues to benefit from a strong institutional framework 
that promotes fiscal discipline, and a modest public-sector debt burden. 
     -- We are therefore affirming our 'AAA/A-1+' ratings on Denmark. 
     -- The outlook remains stable. 
 
RATING ACTION 
On March 8, 2019, S&P Global Ratings affirmed its unsolicited 'AAA' long-term 
and 'A-1+' short-term foreign and local currency sovereign credit ratings on 
Denmark. The outlook is stable. 
 
OUTLOOK 
The stable outlook reflects our expectation that Denmark's strong economic, 
fiscal, external, and monetary credit metrics can withstand most foreseeable 
shocks. We expect Denmark will maintain low government debt, which we see as 
an important factor to offset some of the risks associated with the country's 
still-high household indebtedness and banks' significant external funding 
needs. 
 
We could lower the rating if we observe material slippages in fiscal or 
economic performance stemming from weaker institutional and policymaking 
capabilities. The rating could also come under pressure if the stability of 
the Danish financial sector was jeopardized by worsening asset quality in the 
highly indebted private sector, or if external financing comes under pressure. 
 
RATIONALE 
The rating reflects our view of Denmark's mature political and institutional 
framework, which promotes economic prosperity, competitiveness, and 
flexibility. Longstanding fiscal discipline is also a strength for the rating. 
These factors have supported consistently strong current account surpluses, 
contributing to Denmark's substantial net external asset position. 
Nevertheless, we note potential risks stemming from the financial sector's 
large external borrowing requirements and households' still-high debt, despite 
their deleveraging. 
 
Institutional and economic profile: Strong economic growth amid global slowdown 
     -- We expect the Danish economy will expand by an average of 1.7% in the 
next three years, despite households reducing debt and falling world trade 
possibly weighing on growth in the medium to long term. 
     -- We expect the resilience of Denmark's consensus-led politics to 
continue after the 2019 elections. 
     -- Balanced demand fundamentals and macroprudential efforts cushion risks 
of widening budgetary deficits. 
 
Denmark benefits from a wealthy and diversified economy. Its GDP per capita, 
which we estimate at about $61,600 in 2018, is among the highest of all the 
sovereigns we rate. Furthermore, high-value-added sectors dominate the 
economy, the workforce is skilled and flexible, and the labor participation 
rate is high. 
 
The low GDP growth rate in 2018 does not reflect an accurate picture of the 
economy's underlying performance, due to patent payments in 2017 inflating 
both exports and GDP. We expect growth to pick up in 2019, during which 
exports should expand and a better growing season for the agriculture sector 
is likely. Over 2020-2021, we think that economic progress will continue, 
supported by strong employment growth, steadily rising disposable incomes, and 
low interest rates. Moreover, we think that increasing financial wealth will 
foster private consumption and economic growth in the coming years. 
 
We believe the minority government has been successful in implementing 
measures to counteract risks from the tightening labor market, which in turn 
will enhance growth prospects and help ensure the government's long-term 
financial strength. The measures--which include reforms that increased the 
pension age and incentivized the inflow of mainly skilled foreign labor--have 
helped increase the workforce. That said, we believe employment is nearing 
full capacity, which could dampen Denmark's economic growth. 
 
We note that households have been deleveraging and increasingly moving to 
fixed-rate mortgages over the past few years, thereby reducing their 
sensitivity to interest rate hikes. But even though gross household debt to 
disposable income has reduced from the 2009 peak of 270% to about 215% in late 
2018, Denmark's ratio of bank credit to the resident private sector is the 
highest among European peers. However, thanks to sizable assets, mainly in the 
form of real estate and pension savings, supported by tax benefits, household 
wealth on a net basis is strong. 
 
We don't anticipate significant demand-led imbalances, as was the case before 
the property market slump in 2008. Even though property prices have surpassed 
pre-2008 levels, credit growth has stayed modest, suggesting that house prices 
are not fueled by excessive lending. In addition, growth in consumption and 
investment levels has been moderate. This, together with the high savings 
rate, helps prevent potential overheating. Moreover, a change in the property 
tax from 2021 will restore the link between property values and the tax 
levied, which we believe will strengthen the automatic stabilizers in the real 
estate market. In addition, we have seen several initiatives to contain 
household indebtedness over the past years, through lowered deductibility of 
interest payments, rules supporting fixed-rate debt, and amortization for high 
loan-to-value ratios, and thresholds on debt-to-income ratios. These measures 
specifically affect the property markets of Copenhagen and Aarhus, where real 
estate prices tend to be higher. 
 
Denmark's Liberal-led, minority government must seek coalition partnerships to 
guide legislation through parliament. We note that it gained sufficient 
support to pass its budget for 2019. We also acknowledge the government's 
success in obtaining support for key policies, including the new property tax 
and pension reform. We view Denmark's consensus-led political landscape as 
supportive of the rating, since the current situation presents little risk to 
effective decision-making, despite it being a minority government. We believe 
consensus-based policies will continue after the 2019 election. We consider 
that Denmark's strict budgetary framework prevents excessive spending or 
material structural fiscal deficits. 
 
Following the publication of the "Report on the Non-Resident Portfolio at 
Danske Bank 's Estonian branch", which revealed suspicious transactions of 
around EUR200 billion, Danish and European authorities are following up with a 
number of further investigations to examine the effectiveness of cross-border 
financial regulations. Should the investigations reveal any institutional 
weakness or governance issue, we expect effective countermeasures will be 
implemented in a timely manner. 
 
Flexibility and performance profile: Substantial current account surpluses 
enhance the external position 
     -- Denmark enjoys very strong current account surpluses on the back of 
solid trade balances and robust investment revenues from overseas assets, 
although at a lower level than in past years. 
     -- Low public debt, despite public housing coming onto the central 
government balance sheet, provides strong fiscal flexibility. 
     -- Predictable central bank response patterns continue to uphold the 
krone's peg to the euro. 
 
Denmark's external performance continues to enhance its net creditor position. 
For more than two decades, Denmark has posted particularly strong current 
account surpluses, peaking at about 9% of GDP in 2014. Stagnating exports in 
2018 led to a decrease in the current account surplus to 5.5% of GDP, which we 
believe will pick up in 2019 and remain around 6.0%. 
 
High external savings, as shown by a net external asset position of about 100% 
of current account receipts (CARs) at year-end 2018, continue to generate 
substantial net investment income. The large income surplus supports continued 
strong current account positions. 
 
Using a narrower measure of Denmark's international investment position, we 
estimate that external debt, net of public- and financial-sector assets, will 
average 47.6% of CARs in 2019-2022, down from about 52% in 2016. We forecast 
current account payments plus short-term debt repayments will remain stable at 
about 184% of CARs plus official reserves in 2019. Roughly three-quarters of 
Denmark's external debt is owed by its financial sector. 
 
Denmark's monetary policy is, in our view, limited by the peg of the krone to 
the euro, in contrast to policy of sovereigns with floating and more actively 
traded currencies. Following the strain on Denmark's currency peg in the first 
half of 2015, monetary policy has normalized, with the monetary policy rate 
0.25 percentage points below the European Central Bank 's (ECB 's) policy rate. 
Periods of international uncertainty typically increase investors' appetite 
for the Danish krone, increasing the likelihood of appreciation pressure. In 
early 2019, Denmark's central bank  had to intervene to support the krone. If 
the krone continues to weaken, we would expect Denmark's central bank  to 
support it by raising the interest rate on par with that of the ECB . 
 
We consider Denmark's fiscal policy track record to be strong. For 2018, we 
expect a headline fiscal surplus of 0.2% of GDP. Because the government is 
seeking to contain expenditures and has reduced taxes, we see potential for 
additional growth-boosting reforms. These include further tax reductions, 
property tax refunds, and repayments of early retirement contributions. These 
reforms spur consumption, creating extra demand, and increase the capacity of 
the economy. 
 
Denmark has low government debt, thanks to its budgetary performance. As such, 
we expect gross general government debt will remain below 40% of GDP through 
2022. We note that the central government has decided to finance the social 
housing sector directly by purchasing social housing associations' bonds, and

We believe the Danish banking sector overall is stable and represents limited

record sound profitability on the back of limited loan losses and good 
profitability of mortgage lending, while adhering to strict cost controls. 
Although we have observed a decline in the coverage of nonperforming loans, it 
remains higher than pre-crisis level.

text:
15 Sep 2017 16:11 ET  Press Release: S&PGR Affirms Denmark At 'AAA/A-1+'; Outlook Stable


 
 
The following is a press release from Standard & Poor's: 
 
Ratings: 
Foreign and Local Currency: AAA/Stable/A-1+ 
 
For further details see ratings list. 
 
OVERVIEW 
 
     -- We expect Denmark's wealthy, competitive, and diversified economy will 
expand by 2% per year on average during 2017-2020. 
     -- Denmark benefits from high institutional effectiveness, mature 
political and institutional frameworks that promote fiscal discipline, and a 
modest government debt burden. 
     -- We are therefore affirming our 'AAA/A-1+' ratings on Denmark. 
     -- The stable outlook reflects the depth of Denmark's economic, fiscal, 
external, and monetary buffers. 
 
RATING ACTION 
 
On Sept. 15, 2017, S&P Global Ratings affirmed its 'AAA' long-term and 'A-1+' 
short-term foreign and local currency sovereign credit ratings on the Kingdom 
of Denmark. The outlook is stable. 
 
OUTLOOK 
 
The stable outlook reflects our expectation that Denmark's strong economic, 
fiscal, external, and monetary credit measures can withstand most foreseeable 
shocks. We expect that Denmark will maintain low government debt, which we see 
as important to offset some of the risks associated with the country's high 
household debt and banks' significant external funding needs. 
 
We could lower the ratings if policies weakened, leading to slippages in 
fiscal, economic, or external performance. The ratings could also come under 
pressure if high private-sector debt were to jeopardize the stability of 
Denmark's financial sector. We see these scenarios as unlikely to materialize 
over the coming two years, however. 
 
RATIONALE 
 
The ratings reflect our view of Denmark's mature political and institutional 
framework--which promotes economic prosperity, competitiveness, and 
flexibility--as well as long-standing fiscal discipline. These factors have 
supported consistently strong current account surpluses, contributing to 
Denmark's substantial net external asset position. We note some potential risks 
stemming from the financial sector's large external borrowing requirements and 
still-high household debt. 
 
Institutional and economic profile: Capacity constraints dampen the strong 
growth potential 
     -- High economic growth momentum, but labor market shortages are likely to 
limit medium-term growth potential. 
     -- The consensus-led political landscape will be tested in the upcoming 
2018 budget vote as the minority government looks to garner support for tax 
cuts and expenditure containment. 
     -- Balanced demand fundamentals and macroprudential efforts cushion risks 
of widening imbalances. 
 
Denmark benefits from a wealthy and diversified economy. GDP per capita in 
Denmark is among the highest of all the sovereigns we rate, estimated at about 
US$54,800 in 2017. High-value-added sectors dominate the economy, the workforce 
is skilled and flexible, and the labor participation rate is high. At the same 
time, although shrinking, household gross debt to net disposable income stood 
at 292% at year-end 2016, near its 340% peak of 2008. The ratio of bank credit 
to the resident private sector is the highest among countries in the 
Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD). Even so, we note 
that, over the past three years, households have been amortizing debt and 
increasingly moving to fixed-rate mortgage loans, thus reducing their 
sensitivity to interest rate hikes. Moreover, the highest income earners carry 
the largest debt, which mitigates some of the risks. In addition, household net 
wealth is strong, thanks to significant assets primarily in the form of real 
estate and pension savings, which tax-system benefits also encourage. Still, 
most household assets are in the form of illiquid pension account balances and 
real estate. 
 
The Danish economy is exhibiting strong growth momentum, and we estimate 
economic output will expand by 2.3% in 2017, compared with our previous 
forecast of 1.7%. We see meaningful growth contributions from domestic private 
demand, with sound support from the Danish export industry as it benefits from 
the pickup in demand from key trading partners. In addition, the labor market 
remains solid, with employment up by 2.6% in 2016 and continuing its positive 
trend in 2017, and the unemployment rate set to reduce to 6.0% by 2019. Yet 
despite the healthy labor market, wage increases have been kept in check, 
sustaining Denmark's overall competitiveness. We note high confidence levels 
among households and industries, suggesting that growth will remain sound 
through 2018. 
 
We believe measures to counteract risks from the tightening labor market could 
help maintain the positive momentum of the business cycle. For instance, recent 
reforms that have raised the early retirement age, alongside an inflow of 
foreign labor, have contributed to expansion of the labor force. Yet we foresee 
labor capacity constraints dampening growth potential in 2018-2020, possibly 
reducing GDP growth to around 2%. 
 
We consider the current upswing to be solid and well balanced, so we don't 
anticipate mounting demand-led imbalances, as occurred during the years leading 
up to the sharp correction in the Danish property market in 2008. Even though 
we observe a pickup in the real estate market, with house prices surpassing 
pre-2008 levels, credit growth remains modest, suggesting that house prices are 
not being fuelled by excessive lending. In addition, consumption and investment 
ratios, although increasing, are moderate, which together with sound savings 
help prevent overheating. Moreover, we note that a change in the property tax 
from 2021 will restore the link between property value and the tax being 
levied, which we believe will strengthen the automatic stabilizers in the real 
esate market. In addition, macroprudential measures targeting the property 
markets of Copenhagen and Aarhus will likely curb price increases. 
 
Denmark's minority coalition government needs to seek partnerships to guide 
legislation through parliament. This situation is not unusual in Denmark's 
consensus-led political landscape, suggesting that the current political 
situation presents little risk to effective decision-making. Importantly, we 
observe that political and institutional frameworks, including a strict 
budgetary framework, allow for high institutional effectiveness and government 
discipline, thereby avoiding excessive spending or material structural fiscal 
deficits. Even if elections were held early, which is not our base case, we do 
not expect this would have a material adverse impact on Denmark's institutional 
and policy effectiveness. We observe that the current government has recently 
succeeded in obtaining support for key policies, including the new property tax 
and pension reform, to make it more attractive to stay in the labor market. 
 
Amid the buoyant economic growth, government has presented a 2018 budget bill 
focused on tax cuts and expenditure containment in efforts to extend the 
economic upswing. The proposed tax cuts totaling Danish krone (DKK) 23 billion 
(about $3 billion or 1% of GDP) are intended to be offset by expenditure 
reductions so as not to provide unnecessary fiscal stimulus to the economy. But 
the government might still face challenges in attaining the necessary 
parliamentary support. There is a possibility that the government won't be able 
to push through its expenditure containment plan, meaning further fiscal 
stimulus if the tax cuts are approved. On the other hand, the recent pension 
reform could extend the labor supply by adding flexibility to retirement 
savings, thereby increasing the incentive for the core labor force to remain 
active. 
 
Flexibility and performance profile: A strong external position and low public 
debt provide ample flexibility 
     -- Very strong current account surpluses on the back of solid trade 
balances and robust investment revenues from overseas assets. 
     -- Low public debt provides strong fiscal flexibility, enabling public 
housing financing to move onto the central government balance sheet. 
     -- Predictable central bank response patterns continue to stave off 
appreciation of the krone. 
 
Denmark's external performance continues to enhance its net creditor position. 
For more than two decades, Denmark has posted current account surpluses, which 
were particularly strong in recent years, peaking at about 9% of GDP in 2015. 
We project that the current account surplus will average about 8% of GDP 
annually in 2017-2020, reflecting sound services, goods exports, and, in 
particular, robust net income from sizable external assets. We expect net 
exports will help the current account surplus surpass 8% of GDP in 2017, but 
that rising imports, as the economic cycle progresses, will gradually limit the 
trade balance's contribution to the current account. However, in 2018-2020, 
significant current income from Denmark's net wealth relative to other 
countries, as shown by a net external asset position of about 90% of current 
account receipts (CARs) at year-end 2016, will support the current account. 
 
Using a narrower measure of Denmark's international investment position, we 
estimate that external debt, net of public- and financial-sector assets, will 
average 41% of CARs in 2017-2020, down from about 50% in 2016. We forecast 
current account payments plus short-term debt repayments will decline to about 
180% of CARs plus official reserves in 2017, from 220% in 2010. Roughly 
three-fifths of Denmark's external debt is owed by its financial sector. 
 
In this context, it is important to note that Danske Bank has decided to turn 
its Finnish subsidiary into a branch under the Danish headquarters. Moreover, 
Nordea Bank has changed its legal structure by redefining its subsidiaries in 
Norway, Finland, and Denmark as branches and, more recently, has announced it 
will move its base to Finland in 2018. We note that Nordea Kredit Realkredit, 
Nordea's Danish covered bond entity, will remain in Denmark and hence its

assets and liabilities will not be transferred to the head office. We do not 
anticipate any major impact from these changes on Denmark's external positions 
or gross external financing needs. 
 
The krone is pegged to the euro, which, in our opinion, limits Denmark's 
monetary flexibility compared with that of sovereigns with floating and more 
actively traded currencies, and financial sectors that are better equipped to 
manage currency risk. Following the pressure on Denmark's currency peg in the 
first half of 2015, monetary policy has gradually normalized, with the monetary 
policy rate spread to the eurozone currently negative 0.25 percentage points. 
Periods of international uncertainty typically increase investors' appetite for 
Danish krone, leading to appreciation pressures. We observe that Danmarks 
Nationalbank (DNB), Denmark's central bank, has intervened in the foreign 
currency market albeit to a modest extent. We expect the DNB will counteract 
any upward pressure on the krone in a similar fashion by increasing foreign 
currency reserves and moving its policy rate further into negative territory. 
 
We consider Denmark's fiscal policy track record to be strong. For 2017 and 
2018, we expect a headline fiscal deficit of 1.4% of GDP and 1.2% of GDP, 
respectively. We believe the current strong economic growth could allow for 
more rapid budgetary consolidation than envisaged in the proposed budget bill. 
 
As a result of Denmark's budgetary performance, there is low government debt. 
In recent years, the government has reduced its treasury reserves, which we 
forecast will approach DKK100 billion by year-end 2017, equivalent to about 5% 
of GDP or just over one year of estimated bond redemptions. As such, we expect 
gross general government debt will remain below 40% of GDP through 2020, with 
net debt at about 24%, reflecting sizable liquid assets. In view of its solid 
financial position, the Danish government has recently proposed the possibility 
of financing public housing construction through onlending from the central 
treasury. This would change the current situation, in which public housing 
companies issue mortgage loans covered by public guarantees, predominantly from 
municipalities. We expect a decision in the second half of 2017, following 
which, yearly loan volumes of DKK20 billion could be added to the central 
government's funding requirement, with a corresponding reduction in mortgage 
bank lending. Although this change would translate into a direct liability of 
the central government, we consider that the government has ample room to 
manage a debt increase of this magnitude, given its currently low debt and 
consolidating fiscal trajectory. 
 
We believe the situation in the Danish banking sector is stable and that it 
represents limited contingent liabilities to the sovereign. In addition, 
Denmark's implementation of the EU-wide Banking Recovery and Resolution 
Directive on June 1, 2015, has reduced the central government's contingent 
liabilities, in our view, since we expect the Danish authorities will use the 
bail-in tool to resolve deposit-taking banks, if necessary. The authorities 
also require mortgage lending institutions to hold a bail-in-able buffer of 2% 
of mortgage loans to avoid government bailouts of large systemic banking 
groups. The banking sector continues to record sound profitability on the back 
of lower loan losses and increased profitability of mortgage lending, while 
adhering to strict cost control. In particular, we note that impairment charges 
are currently at their lowest level since 2007, and evolving customer 
preferences toward digital solutions have allowed for reduced staff and 
branches. We expect some further expansion of the duration of wholesale funding 
as mortgage providers continue to transfer clients to longer-dated financing 
options to limit refinancing risk. But we note that the average duration of 
Danish bank's wholesale funding already exceeds that of Nordic peers by a wide 
margin.

title: Euro Eases Franc's Strain -- WSJ
text:
This article is being republished as part of our daily reproduction of WSJ.com articles that also appeared in the U.S. print edition of The Wall Street Journal (July 8, 2017).

ZURICH -- The yearslong battle that smaller European central banks have waged against their own strong currencies may have turned a corner, thanks to the strengthening euro.

Increased confidence in the eurozone, both politically and economically, has raised the euro's value against a broad swath of big and small currencies, including some of its neighbors. Amid these improved prospects for Europe, central bankers in Switzerland, Denmark and the Czech Republic have dramatically scaled back their purchases of foreign currencies in recent months.

The Swiss National Bank's foreign-exchange reserves -- accumulated on a massive scale since 2012 -- dipped slightly last month to 693.5 billion Swiss francs ($721 billion), the SNB said Friday. The figures suggest the central bank has pulled back on its currency intervention efforts.

Denmark hasn't intervened in markets since March, according to central bank data. Data from the Czech central bank showed currency intervention of just EUR653 million ($745 million) in April, down sharply from March.

This is in contrast to the first quarter, when these banks cumulatively added tens of billions of dollars' worth of foreign currency to their balance sheets. By creating new Swiss francs, Danish kroner and Czech koruna and using them to buy foreign currency assets, these central banks hoped to weaken their own currencies and protect exporters while boosting inflation.

Their ability to step back is a byproduct of the broader normalization occurring among big central banks. The Federal Reserve has raised rates twice this year and is expected to do so again before year-end. The European Central Bank has reduced its quantitative easing program, and officials have sounded more positive about the bloc's economic outlook, even though its deposit rate is still negative.

This has the potential to reduce demand for assets in countries such as Switzerland, whose currencies tend to benefit amid uncertain times in the global economy.

"The Danes and Swiss are all at the mercy of large central banks. Sometimes they lose, like when the ECB cut rates into negative territory and sometimes it works in their favor," as is the case more recently, said Peter Rosenstreich, head of market strategy at Swissquote Bank.

Switzerland has battled the strong franc since the euro crisis intensified in 2010, prompting its central bank to spend vast sums intervening and, eventually, setting a ceiling on the franc's strength in 2011. When it abandoned that cap in early 2015, it was forced to step up its intervention.

Denmark, meanwhile, has a target range for the euro-kroner exchange rate. The Czech central bank had a euro target for a while, but dropped it in April.

The euro traded at just under 1.10 Swiss francs early Friday, near a one-year high. The euro fetched 7.44 kroner -- which is near the middle of the Danish central bank's target range -- and 26.1 Czech koruna, just slightly weaker than when the koruna target was in place.

A strong currency brings many economic benefits. It reflects the confidence global investors attach to assets of countries such as Switzerland, which is known as a haven. It raises purchasing power and may make key imported commodities like oil less expensive.

But when it is too strong, the economy may slide into persistent consumer price declines known as deflation, which weakens consumption and investment. A strong currency also typically damps exports.

And the exchange rate effects extend beyond exports and consumer prices. The Czech Republic is a key manufacturing hub in sectors like automobiles and thus benefits from low costs. Switzerland is home to global corporate powerhouses like Nestlé SA and Swatch Group AG which generate a significant share of their revenue from overseas but report their earnings in francs.

Switzerland's central bank "is breathing a sigh of relief," said Mr. Rosenstreich.

title: Why Are Europe’s Small Central Banks Stocking Up Foreign Money?
text:
ZURICH—Europe’s smaller central banks are loading up on foreign currencies at rates usually associated with periods of intense global stress, highlighting the fragile underpinnings of the global economic recovery despite the recent upbeat mood in financial markets.

Switzerland’s holdings of foreign assets jumped last month at their fastest pace in over two years as its central bank fought the strong franc, which weakens exports and inflation. The Czech central bankintervened in January on a massive scale to maintain its currency target against the euro. Denmark has also stepped up its foreign-currency purchases to keep the krone from strengthening too much.

These central banks are showing crisis-like behavior to protect their currencies even in the absence of obvious trouble. This exposes them to losses if their currencies fail to weaken on their own. It also raises doubts as to how long they can keep this up in an era when economic and political uncertainties appear to be a lasting feature of the world economy.

“There is a little bit of survivor behavior,” said Peter Rosenstreich, head of market strategy at Swissquote Bank. “They’ve been protecting their currencies so long and it’s hard to give up that defensive position.”

The Swiss National Bank said Tuesday its foreign exchange reserves swelled nearly 25 billion Swiss francs ($24.63 billion) last month to 668 billion francs, the biggest rise since December 2014, the month before the Swiss abandoned a cap on the franc’s value. The pile of foreign reserves is greater than Switzerland’s entire gross domestic product.

“It’s quite bizarre. You’d think at some time you’d run out of surprises,” said Stefan Gerlach, chief economist at BSI Bank in Zurich and a former deputy governor at Ireland’s central bank.

The franc is regarded as one of the world’s safest currencies given Switzerland’s stable economy and low debt, meaning its value usually increases when investors seek safety instead of returns.

Analysts cited elections in France this spring, in Germany this fall and continued political uncertainty in Italy, the U.S. and U.K. as reasons for the relentless demand for the franc and other safe-haven currencies.

Central banks accumulate foreign reserves when they purchase assets denominated in other currencies, using freshly created money. They do this to weaken their currencies, protecting exports and giving a boost to inflation. Foreign reserves can waver slightly due to changes in currency values, but big increases like Switzerland’s signal aggressive intervention.

This tool has gained traction in recent years as official rates have turned negative in Denmark and Switzerland and are near zero in the Czech Republic.

The Czech central bank said Tuesday that currency intervention was 14.5 billion euros ($15.3 billion) in January, the largest amount by far since it introduced an exchange rate target against the euro in November 2013. “It is an eye-popping number,” said Bruna Skarica, economist at Oxford Economics.

Czech officials have said they plan to discontinue this target in the middle of this year, which has spurred investor flows into the Czech currency, the koruna, in anticipation.

Denmark intervened last month to the tune of 4.7 billion kroner ($670 million), the most since last June.

Like the franc, the Danish krone typically rises in uncertain times, especially in the eurozone. The Czech Republic is seen as one of the more stable economies within central and Eastern Europe, so it sees similar trends.

What sets this latest episode apart is that there wasn’t a particular destabilizing stress point in the last few weeks like the Greek crisis or the U.K. vote to leave the European Union. Global markets have been mostly calm with U.S. equities marking record highs. Government bond yields have risen but not too much.

Meanwhile, the U.S. Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank are close to hitting their 2% inflation targets, and the Fed is expected to raise interest rates as soon as next week.

This should be a recipe for reduced demand for the Swiss, Danish and Czech currencies as investors seek higher returns elsewhere. But the opposite has occurred.

The euro traded at 1.0723 francs midday Tuesday, about 10% lower than it was when the SNB had the franc ceiling in place from 2011 to early 2015. The euro fetched 7.43 Danish kroner, which is within the Danish bank’s target of within 2.25% above or below 7.46. The Czech koruna is near the central bank’s target of 27 against the euro, but only due to the massive intervention.

“The global economy is doing better than in the last few years” and has broadened out, SNB Chairman Thomas Jordan said in a Swiss newspaper interview on March 4.

But alluding to the contrast between a better economy and heightened political tension that has bedeviled his central bank, Mr. Jordan noted the political risks are on the rise.

“Such phases of increased political uncertainty are problematic for us because the Swiss franc is considered a safe haven,” he said.

title: UPDATE 1- Denmark  defends its  currency  peg with biggest  intervention  since Brexit
text:
(Adds details, comments, updates dateline)

By Teis Jensen and Jemima Kelly

COPENHAGEN/LONDON, March 2 (Reuters) - Denmark's central bank sold 4.7 billion Danish crowns ($665 million) on the foreign exchange market in February to defend its currency peg amid high demand for crowns from investors worried about the future of the euro.

It was the central bank's biggest intervention since June last year, when it stepped into the market as demand for the Danish currency rose on fears that Britain's shock vote to leave the European Union could have ripple effects in the euro zone.

Under the European Union's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM2), Denmark must keep the crown within 2.25 percent of 7.46038 crowns per euro, although in practice it has not moved more than 0.5 percent either way.

Europe's single currency faces political risks including a French presidential election which anti-euro, far-right leader Marine Le Pen is seen by bookmakers as having a 30 percent chance of winning.

This has prompted some investors to seek alternatives to the euro, and they see Denmark - among a handful of countries with a triple-A credit rating, and with a large surplus in its balance of payments - as a safe bet.

"If Le Pen wins, against expectations, she has announced that there will be a referendum on the euro - that would obviously shake the foundation of the euro cooperation, and that has led investors to seek shelter in Danish crowns," said Nykredit chief economist Tore Stramer, in Copenhagen.

"We will probably have to live with that traffic until (results day) in France on May 8."

With jitters over the French election weighing on the euro, the Danish crown in late February hit its highest levels since the results of June's Brexit vote, at 7.4325 crowns per euro .

"GREAT CONFIDENCE"

February's intervention was detailed by central bank on Thursday. It was dwarfed, however, by the hundreds of billions of crowns sold in early 2015 after the Swiss National Bank scrapped the ceiling on the Swiss franc's exchange rate against the euro, sparking a speculative run on the crown.

That intervention had bolstered investors' faith in the central bank's willingness to defend the crown, analysts said.

"There is a great confidence in the fixed exchange rate policy, which makes investors to some extent enforce (it) themselves because they don't want to buy crowns at too a high price, because they know (it) will fall back closer to the central rate again," said Sydbank economist Soren Kristensen.

He added that the central bank, whose foreign exchange reserves have fallen to levels last seen before the Swiss franc shock, would be willing to intervene far more aggressively if strong upward pressure was put on the Danish crown. It would prefer to do that than further cut its key interest rate, currently at minus 0.65 percent, he said.

The central bank said its total foreign exchange reserves rose to 466.6 billion Danish crowns in February, up from 457.8 billion crowns at the end of January.

title: Denmark Central Bank Currency Intervention  Is Possible -- 1Q  Central Bank  Outlook
text:
The Danish central bank looks unlikely to move interest rates in the first quarter, but it could return to currency markets if the Danish krone's exchange rate begins to veer off target.

Denmark's Nationalbank aims to make life easier for exporters to the important eurozone market, as well as keep inflation low and steady, by tightly controlling the national currency.

It's only policy aim is to keep the euro's exchange rate within 2.25% of 7.46038 kroner.

The krone has been on the strong side over recent weeks and the central bank will have taken note. Analysts expect the bank to react soon and begin selling kroner.

"We do not believe that the bank will allow a further appreciation of the krone," said Jan Storup Nielsen at Nordea Bank in Copenhagen.

Of vital importance for Danish interest rates throughout 2017 will be the actions of the European Central Bank. Further easing in Frankfurt could send the euro lower against the krone and force Danish policy makers into counter measures.

However, as the ECB looks likely to leave its policy levers largely unchanged in the short term, Nationalbank may do likewise.

Mr. Storup Nielsen expects the central bank's key interest rate to remain at minus 0.65% into 2018.

S&P cut the investment-grade credit ratings of the European Union by a notch, saying the U.K.'s vote to leave the EU reduces its budget flexibility and reflects a loss of political solidarity.

China's official manufacturing purchasing managers' index, a gauge of the nation's factory activity, edged down in June, ending three straight months of expansion, official data showed Friday.

The index fell to 50.0--the mark that separates expansion from contraction--from 50.1 a month ago, suggesting the world's second-largest economy is still struggling to gain momentum. The June PMI matched a median forecast of 50.0 by 13 economists polled by The Wall Street Journal.

Turkey opened a new area of membership talks with the European Union on Thursday, but bloc officials made clear there was no prospect of further advancement to Ankara's bid in the coming months.

Turkey had pressed for an advancement of its talks on membership as a condition of the deal to take back migrants who cross into Greece and the EU. The EU fulfilled that pledge by opening what is called a chapter in the accession discussions.

There are 35 chapters in the accession talks. The EU has begun discussion on 16 of them, including the chapter on financial and budgetary provisions which were opened Thursday. But talks on only one chapter have been completed and the EU hasn't opened discussion on any of the most sensitive topics.

Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis President James Bullard said Thursday the U.S. economy was in an era of modest growth that would keep unemployment and inflation at their current levels for the next 2 1/2 years.

"Key macroeconomic variables including real output growth, the unemployment rate, and inflation appear to be at or near values that are likely to persist over the forecast horizon," Mr. Bullard said. "Any further cyclical adjustment is likely to be relatively minor."

By Teis Jensen

COPENHAGEN, June 15 (Reuters) - Denmark is ready to cut interest rates further into negative territory and make unlimited interventions in the currency market if needed to defend the crown's peg to the euro, the head of its central bank said on Wednesday.

Uncertainty over how Britain's referendum on June 23 on whether to stay in the European Union will play out has prompted investors to buy Danish crowns, seen as a safe haven.

That has helped strengthen the currency to the upper end of the tight band to the euro the central bank has kept it within.

The central bank intervened in the currency market in May for the first time in three months, buying foreign reserves and selling its own currency, which helped ease pressure on the crown towards the end of the month.

The Nationalbank is ready for unlimited intervention and to let its reserve of foreign exchange "sky rocket", central bank governor Lars Rohde told a press meeting on Wednesday.

He said the bank could also cut interest rates further, a stronger tool used less often than foreign exchange intervention to weaken the crown. In January the bank raised its certificate of deposit rate to minus 0.65 percent from minus 0.75 percent.

"We did not (reach) the lowest possible rate last year, so there is the possibility to go further into negative territory if needed," Rohde said.

Last year, speculators poured money into the AAA-rated country's currency, betting Denmark would drop the three-decade-old currency peg and let the crown rise, after the Swiss National Bank scrapped its cap on the franc against the euro.

At 1108 GMT, the crown was trading at 7.4357 per euro .

Under the ERM2 Exchange Rate Mechanism, the crown must stay within 2.25 percent of a rate of 7.46038 per euro. In reality the central bank has kept to a much tighter range of plus/minus 0.50 percent. (Additional reporting by Erik Matzen and Jacob Gronholt-Pedersen,; editing by John Stonestreet)

title: INTERVIEW-Danish  central bank  ready to  intervene  if Brexit hits crown
text:
COPENHAGEN, June 3 (Reuters) - Denmark's central bank says it is ready to intervene to weaken the crown if a British exit from the European Union later this month triggers inflows into the Danish currency.

Speculators poured money into AAA-rated country's currency in January and February last year, betting Denmark would drop its three-decade-old currency peg and let the crown rise, after the Swiss National Bank scrapped its cap on the franc against the euro.

Upward pressure on the Danish crown since early March has led the central bank to buy almost 24 billion crowns ($3.7 billion)worth of foreign currency in May.

"We cannot rule out that an inflow of currency can happen if the British vote no at the referendum," central bank Governor Per Callesen said on the sidelines of a Thomson Reuters banking seminar in Copenhagen.

Callesen said the central bank is standing firm on the current Danish currency regime, which pegs the value of the crown to the euro.

"We don't see anyone in the political sphere or media pushing for a change in the regime. We believe we have the means available for keeping the exchange rate," Callesen said.

Intervention in currency markets is the tool the central bank uses most to defend the peg. It has also raised the possibility of adjusting interest rates independently of the European Central Bank.

Callesen underscored that potential pressure on the crown would be different from what happened last year, when Switzerland changed its exchange rate regime.

"The referendum in Britain will not have any impact on the exchange regime," Callesen said.

The Danish central bank said on Thursday foreign exchange reserves rose to 426.9 billion Danish crowns in May from 403.5 billion crowns a month earlier.

The central bank also said it intervened in forex marked by selling 23.6 billion crowns to keep the currency stable against the euro. It was the first intervention since February.

Under the Exchange Rate Mechanism, Denmark must keep the crown within 2.25 percent of a rate of 7.46038 per euro. In practice, it has kept to a much tighter range of plus or minus 0.50 percent. title: UPDATE 2-Denmark hikes main rate to keep crown in tight range vs euro
text:
(Adds analyst, currency move, context)

By Sabina Zawadzki

COPENHAGEN, Jan 7 (Reuters) - Denmark's central bank raised its main interest rate on Thursday to keep its currency in a tight range against the euro, in a rare step taken independently of action by the European Central Bank, with which it usually moves in lockstep.

In its first move since last February, the bank raised its certificate of deposit rate to minus 0.65 percent from minus 0.75 percent. It left its lending and discount rates at 0.05 percent and 0.00 percent, respectively.

It uses the deposit rate, the return banks get for parking money with it for one week, as one way to maintain the Danish crown's long-held peg to the euro. The central bank also frequently intervenes in foreign currency markets.

Thursday's move follows nine consecutive months of interventions to bolster the crown as well as Denmark failing to act when the ECB cut rates on Dec. 3.

The rate hike is also out of step with neighbouring Sweden, which has been battling flat or falling consumer prices and said earlier this week it was ready to intervene in currency markets despite the fact that the Swedish crown floats freely.

The Danish crown has traded around 7.4610 per euro in recent days, close to its central parity rate of 7.46038, although it strengthened to a two-month high at 7.4575 following the rate decision.

The central bank has no fixed schedule of meetings and never gives guidance on monetary policy. But many analysts had expected Thursday's move in view of the amounts the central bank has spent on intervention.

"Whether today's rate hike will be followed by further rate hikes will depend entirely on the future development of the Danish crown against the euro. In our main scenario we do not expect that further rate increases will be required on this side of summer," said Nordea's chief analyst, Jan Storup Nielsen.

DENMARK WINS 'CROWN WAR'

Denmark began diverging from European Central Bank actions at the start of last year when the crown came under huge upward pressure from investors believing the country would drop the euro peg, days after Switzerland scrapped its cap on the franc against the shared currency.

That pressure eased after four rate cuts in January and February, massive interventions and other moves such as the suspension of government bond issues. On April 2 the crown hit its weakest point against the euro in 14 years.

Since then, the central bank has gradually depleted its foreign currency reserves as it fights the weakness of the crown through intervention.

"Today's interest rate announcement is yet another sign that the crown war has found its final closure," said Christian Heinig, chief economist at Realkredit Danmark, referring to the pressure on the currency in the wake of Switzerland's move.

"A closure was already indicated in 2015 as foreign exchange reserves declined, and it became even more evident in December when the central bank did not copy the interest rate cut from the European Central Bank," he said.

Data issued on Tuesday showed the bank's reserves fell by almost 50 billion crowns in December, the largest drop since Lehman Brothers collapsed in 2008.

Its reserves are now lower than at the end of 2014, when the crown began to strengthen causing the central bank to pump crowns into the market by buying foreign currency, thus building the reserves to record highs.

Reserves fell by 49 billion crowns to 434.9 billion crowns ($62.7 billion) in December from 483.9 billion crowns at the end of November having peaked at 737 billion crowns last March.

Under the European Union's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM2), Denmark, an EU member but euro zone outsider, has agreed to keep the crown within 2.25 percent of the parity rate of 7.46038 crowns to the euro. In practice, the crown has not moved more than 0.5 percent either side of that rate.

"Central bank head Lars Rohde can now be euphoric after the victory. The war on the crown, which raged in the beginning of 2015, is now over with the Central Bank as a clear winner," Sydbank's chief economist, Jacob Graven, said. (Additional reporting by Teis Jensen and Annabela Nielsen, editing by Hugh Lawson)

title: Danish rate hike may be coming after  central bank interventions
text:
COPENHAGEN, Dec 17 (Reuters) - Denmark's central bank has spent 25 billion to 30 billion crowns ($4.4 billion) this month to maintain the currency's peg to the euro, an effort that may trigger a rise in interest rates, perhaps as early as Thursday, some analysts said.

Central bank efforts to keep its currency linked to the euro led it to slash rates and sell crowns earlier this year to weaken the crown. Lately, though, it has had to buy crowns to keep its value closer to the euro's. A rate increase, which would also strengthen the crown, would be the logical next move.

Even the modest increase expected by most analysts would move Danish monetary policy in the opposite direction to the European Central Bank's. The ECB cut its deposit rate by 0.10 percentage point earlier in December.

Because the Danish crown is linked to the euro in a narrow range, the central bank usually conducts the same monetary policy as the ECB and normally changes rates on the same day as the ECB. But it sat out the ECB's Dec. 3 rate cut.

Since the ECB rate decision, analysts estimate the central bank has spent more of its foreign currency reserves, meaning it intervened in the market to strengthen the crown.

"We now forecast that over the next three months the Danish central bank will hike the certificates of deposit rate by a modest 10 basis points to -0.65 percent," Danske Bank wrote.

"An independent rate hike could potentially come as early as today," it wrote in a note to clients on Thursday.

Denmark's central bank has no scheduled rate-setting meetings. But rate changes tend to be announced on Thursdays at 1500 GMT.

Chief economist Jes Asmussen at Handelsbanken Markets estimates the central bank's intervention at 30 billion crowns. Nordea Markets puts it at 25 billion.

"The currency reserves might be back on pre-crisis levels within the next couple of months, which may open up for an independent Danish rate hike," Nordea wrote in a note.

Denmark's certificate of deposit rate has been deep in negative territory since early February, at -0.75 percent. The ECB lowered its deposit rate by 10 basis points to -0.3 percent.

Four interest rate cuts in January and February to keep the crown within its euro range after strong pressure on the national currency has resulted in record low rates.

To keep at bay speculators betting Denmark will scrap the euro peg, the central bank flooded the market with crowns, building up foreign currency reserves. It also called off government bond issues to ease demand for Danish assets.

Its reserves peaked at a record of 737 billion Danish crowns ($107 billion) in March. By the end of November, reserves amounted to 484 billion crowns, not far off the at 447 billion seen at the end of last year, before the pressure on the crown.

COPENHAGEN, Oct 1 (Reuters) - Speculation against the Danish crown has usually resulted in a downward pressure, but upward pressure is more likely in the future, the central bank governor said.

"Denmark's role as a creditor nation, where the balance is in our favour, means that future crown crises are likely more often to result in upward pressure," Governor Lars Rohde said in a speech on Thursday.

Speculators poured money into Danish assets at the start of the year, betting that Denmark would drop its three-decade-old currency peg to the euro, following a move by the Swiss central bank to scrap its cap on the franc against the euro.

That pressure led Denmark to cut interest rates, intervene heavily in the foreign exchange market and suspend government debt issuance in a bid to relieve demand for the crown.

Capital flows in January and February were greater than they were earlier, which reflects a trend with the crown, Rohde said. Changes in interest rates have more effect when the crown is weakening, he said, while intervention in the foreign exchange market have more impact when money is flowing in, Rohde said.

Denmark's benchmark certificate of deposit rate has been at -0.75 percent, compared with the ECB's deposit rate of -0.2 percent, since February. It was cut four times in less than two months when the crown was being forced up.

Rohde said on Sept. 16 that the money markets appear to be pricing in an interest rate increase, but he declined to say when and by how much the bank will lift its main rate.

title: UPDATE 2-Danish  central bank  chief says market counting on rate hike
text:
(Releads on rate expectations, adds cbank governor comments)

By Ole Mikkelsen

COPENHAGEN, Sept 16 (Reuters) - Danish central bank governor Lars Rohde said on Wednesday the money markets appear to be pricing in an interest rate hike, but he declined to say when and by how much the bank will lift its main rate.

The spread in the money market for one-month interest rates between Denmark and the euro zone has narrowed to -0.2 percentage points from -0.8 points in February, showing that investors expect Danish rates to be closer to their ECB peers.

Denmark's benchmark, the certificate of deposit rate, has been at -0.75 percent, compared with the ECB's deposit rate of -0.2 percent, since February after four cuts in less than two months when the crown currency came under heavy pressure to strengthen.

"The negative spread to the euro area in the Danish money market has become smaller. One could interpret it as the market's expectation for gradual increases in interest rates," Rohde told reporters.

Some Danish analysts expect a rate hike could come at any time while others see a rise or two by the end of the year.

Speculators poured money into Danish assets at the start of the year, betting Denmark would drop its three-decade-old currency peg, following a move by the Swiss central bank to scrap its cap on the franc against the euro.

That pressure lead Denmark to cut interest rates, intervene heavily in the foreign exchange market and suspend government debt issuance in a bid to relieve demand for the crown.

The government plans to resume bond issuance as of October, but the central bank said it would not hesitate to suspend issuance again if need be.

"We have plenty of tools to achieve the objective of keeping the crown stable," Rohde told Reuters after the bank issued its quarterly economic forecasts.

ECONOMIC UPSWING

The bank trimmed its forecast for economic growth in 2015 but said overall the country was heading for an upswing and the government should move away from fiscal stimulus policies.

It expected the economy to grow 1.8 percent this year, lower than its previous forecast of 2.0 percent, mainly because of lower exports and private consumption earlier this year. It kept its 2016 forecast at 2.1 percent.

It said Denmark's growth potential is between 1.0 percent and 1.3 percent per year with a steady workforce and the country needed more in employment to reach stronger growth rates such the forecasted 1.8 percent for this year. The labour markets has improved with an increasing work force in 26 consecutive months.

Denmark's economy is largely export-driven, so it depends on the fortunes of neighbours such as Germany and Sweden, the largest buyers of its goods.

A new centre-right government has been in place since July and promised to freeze state spending at current levels, although it relies on support in parliament of the populist Danish People's Party, who advocate more spending. title: Europe's Central Bankers Hit Calmer Waters
text:
The Wall Street Journal's Daily Report on Global Central Banks for Wednesday, April 8, 2015:

Sign up for the newsletter: http://on.wsj.com/grandcentralsignup ("http://on.wsj.com/grandcentralsignup")

Highlights

-- Blackstone's Take: Europe's Central Bankers Hit Calmer Waters

-- Kocherlakota Says Fed Should Be "Extraordinarily Patient" On Rates

-- 5 Things to Watch in the Fed's March Minutes

-- Bank of Japan Votes Down Call to Slash Easing

-- Ukraine in Talks to Boost Emergency Cash Reserves

BLACKSTONE'S TAKE: EUROPE'S CENTRAL BANKERS HIT CALMER WATERS

After a topsy-turvy start to 2015, Europe's central banks appear to have found their footing.

The European Central Bank said Tuesday that it hit its monthly target of 60 billion euros ($65.1 billion) in bond purchases in March, the first month of its new quantitative easing program.

This occurred despite the fact that government bond purchases only began on March 9, and helped to alleviate concerns that the ECB won't be able to find sufficient assets to buy to meet its ambitious goal of EUR1.1 trillion in asset purchases by September 2016.

And things have stabilized in smaller European countries whose currencies had been rocked by the ECB's QE program. Denmark's central bank--which intervened massively in currency markets in January and February to keep the krone from strengthening too much against the euro--didn't intervene last month, the bank said Tuesday.

In Switzerland, where a soaring franc early this year fueled concerns of deflation, consumer prices fell less than expected in March on an annual basis, by 0.9% versus market expectations of a 1.1% drop. That will likely reduce pressure on the Swiss National Bank to take additional unconventional easing steps, such as deeper cuts to its already negative deposit rate.

This week's reports support the prevailing view that the focus of financial markets will shift away from Europe in coming months and toward the Federal Reserve, which will decide as soon as June whether to raise interest rates for the first time in nearly a decade.

Still, if the past few years in Europe are any indication, the calm could prove fleeting. A rising share of the eurozone government debt market trades at negative yields-- Spain joined the club Tuesday with a negative rate on six-month T-bills--which could make it harder down for the road for the ECB to buy large amounts of government bonds unless it pays a high premium for them.

And any hiccups from Greece or elsewhere in the eurozone could put renewed upward pressure on currencies in Denmark, Sweden and Switzerland, forcing those central banks to respond.

But for now, central bankers in Europe should welcome the reprieve, however long it lasts.

-By Brian Blackstone

MORNING MINUTES: KEY DEVELOPMENTS AROUND THE WORLD

Kocherlakota Says Fed Should Be "Extraordinarily Patient" On Rates. The Federal Reserve should hold off on raising interest rates until the second half of 2016, Minneapolis Fed President Narayana Kocherlakota said Tuesday. "Under my current outlook, I continue to believe that it would be a mistake to raise the target range for the fed funds rate in 2015," he said.

5 Things to Watch in the Fed's March Minutes. The Fed last month gave itself the option of raising interest rates in June, but also signaled it will remain cautious about actually pulling the trigger. More clues about the debate inside the U.S. central bank could be revealed when the Fed releases minutes of its March 17-18 policy meeting. Here's what to watch when they come out Wednesday at 2 p.m. EDT.

Fed's Bear Stearns, JPMorgan, AIG Bailout Records Remain Secret -- Courthouse News Service. Federal Reserve memos and spreadsheets regarding emergency loans to three big financial firms during the 2008 crisis are not subject to release under the Freedom of Information Act, a federal judge ruled Tuesday.

Dollar Coin Loses Currency on Savings. At one time, the U.S. could have saved billions by ditching the flimsy dollar bill in favor of a durable coin. But for a dollar coin to succeed, the dollar bill needed to be eliminated. Now, the lifespan of paper money has increased, the bulk of the potential savings has been forfeited and the U.S. Federal Reserve, which once supported the change, is against it.

ECB Hits Its March Bond-Purchase Target. The European Central Bank reached its target of EUR60 billion in monthly bond purchases under a new stimulus program launched in March, a sign of resolve that the bank will eventually pump more than EUR1 trillion in freshly created money to stoke the European economy and boost inflation.

ECB's Mersch Shoots Down Speculation of Deposit Rate Cut--Boersen-Zeitung. ECB executive board member Yves Mersch rejects speculation the bank could cut its deposit rate below the current rate of -0.2%. He said in an interview with German newspaper Boersen-Zeitung, "From my point of view, a cost-benefit analysis rules out another cut in the deposit rate." --Dow Jones Newswires.

Bank of Japan Votes Down Call to Slash Easing. The Bank of Japan's internal split widened Wednesday, as Gov. Haruhiko Kuroda's toughest critic on the policy board officially called for a steep reduction of its aggressive monetary stimulus.

Denmark Stays Out of Currency Market. Denmark's central bank refrained from intervening in the foreign-exchange market in March, in a sign that the national currency has stabilized against the euro following weeks of volatility brought on by the European Central Bank's stimulus efforts.

Bank of Russia Sees No Ruble-Related Risks to Financial Stability. The Bank of Russia sees no risks to financial stability from volatility in the ruble, which has firmed to levels last seen in late December, the head of the monetary policy department at the bank said on Wednesday --Dow Jones Newswires.

Ukraine in Talks to Boost Emergency Cash Reserves. Ukraine is in talks with several countries to provide currency swap lines to boost the country's emergency cash reserves, the International Monetary Fund's No. 2 official, David Lipton, said Tuesday.

Hungary's Central Bank to Build Portfolio of Chinese Yuan Bonds. The Hungarian central bank said Tuesday it had decided to build a bond portfolio denominated in Chinese yuan in a bid to diversify its foreign-currency assets. The move, which will take place in several steps, won't materially influence the adequacy of the central bank's foreign-exchange reserves since the portfolio will be relatively small in size, the National Bank of Hungary said in a statement --Dow Jones Newswires.

Hungary Central Bank Wants Big Rise in Investment Guarantee Limit. Hungary's central bank wants a four-fold increase in the amount of compensation investors would receive for unlawful losses or bankruptcies, the bank said Tuesday, after thousands of retail investors saw big losses following the recent bankruptcies of various locally owned brokerages. The bank has proposed increasing the maximum indemnity payment to 100,000 euros ($109,861) from the current limit of 6 million Hungarian forints ($22,030). --Dow Jones Newswires.

Spain Joins Negative Yield Club. Spain's government on Tuesday issued short-term debt yielding a shade under 0%. The EUR725 million ($796 million) in six-month Spanish debt delivers an average yield to investors of -0.002%. Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Ireland and Austria already have all their short-term debt trading with yields under 0% in the post-issuance market.

India's Central Bank Still Struggling With New GDP Figures. While it's the job of every central bank to find the fine balance between growth and inflation, India's top central banker says he's feeling a bit wobbly, as he's uncertain how to read the country's recently revised gross domestic product numbers.

GRAPHIC CONTENT

How Rich and Poor Spend (and Earn) Their Money. For many Americans, the rise in food and housing prices is a tough squeeze. That's because--even in an era with low overall inflation--low-income Americans spend a disproportionate share of their money on food and housing. New data from the Labor Department show the extent of the discrepancy.

FORWARD GUIDANCE

-8 a.m. EDT: Fed's Powell speaks on "Challenges for Monetary Policy" in New York

-10 a.m. EDT: New York Fed's Dudley speaks in New York

-2 p.m. EDT: Federal Reserve releases minutes from its March 17-18 policy meeting

RESEARCH

Nominal GDP: Target or Benchmark? Robert L. Hetzel wrote in an Economic Brief from the Richmond Fed: "Implemented as an activist rule, nominal GDP targeting could be destabilizing. Even if it were feasible, keeping nominal GDP on a preset path in the face of an inflation shock could initiate a recession, while keeping nominal GDP on a target path left unrevised periodically would force changes in inflation if persistent changes in productivity occurred," Still, he wrote, "articulation of a benchmark path for the level of nominal GDP would be a useful start in formulating and communicating policy as a rule. An explicit rule would in turn highlight the importance of shaping the expectations of markets about the way in which the central bank will behave in the future."

COMMENTARY

On Secular Stagnation, Ben Bernanke's Theory Meets Larry Summers's Evidence. "Two of the biggest names in macroeconomics met on the battlefield of the blogosphere last week," Greg Ip writes for the Journal. "Former Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke and former Treasury Secretary Larry Summers were debating why interest rates are so low. .. They both make persuasive (and entertaining) cases. My read is that Mr. Bernanke has theory on his side, while Mr. Summers has the evidence."

Should Monetary Policy Take Into Account Risks to Financial Stability? "Let there be no mistake: In light of our recent experience, threats to financial stability must be taken extremely seriously," former Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke writes on his blog. "However, as a means of addressing those threats, monetary policy is far from ideal. .. In their efforts to promote financial stability, central banks should focus their efforts on improving their supervisory, regulatory, and macroprudential policy tools."

America's Endless War Over Money. "The "Audit the Fed" debate is the latest manifestation of a conflict as old as the nation, between those who argue that a strong central bank improves economic stability, and those who see an overbearing government engaged in harmful meddling," K evin Granville and Binyamin Appelbaum write in a New York Times illustrated timeline of U.S. central-banking controversies.

BASIS POINTS

- The number of job openings in the U.S. climbed to the highest level in 14 years, surpassing five million for the first time since January 2001. But the number of Americans actually getting hired for jobs fell for the second consecutive month, as did the number of people who voluntarily quit.

- Americans pared their credit-card debt in February, the Fed reported Tuesday. Outstanding consumer credit--reflecting Americans' total debt outside of mortgages--grew in February, but the gain was entirely driven by car loans and education debt rather than credit cards.

- Aging populations and sluggish advances in worker productivity are binding the global economy to a bleaker, low-growth fate, the International Monetary Fund said in a new report Tuesday.

- The Czech central bank, which recently has stepped up its rhetoric warning of possible foreign exchange interventions, on Wednesday said its foreign-exchange reserves at the end of March edged up slightly on the month in euro terms, but fell when measured in U.S. dollars--Dow Jones Newswires.

- Inflationary expectations in Russia have started to stabilize, the central bank monetary policy chief said Wednesday, underpinning expectations that more rate cuts are in the pipeline --Dow Jones Newswires.

- The Reserve Bank of Australia and the People's Bank of China extended a local-currency-swap agreement worth A$40 billion (CNY 200 billion) --Dow Jones Newswires.

- Retail sales in the eurozone fell in February after four successive monthly increases, an indication that the boost to the spending power of households from lower oil prices may be waning.

- The Bank of Portugal has a new smartphone app, available in both Portuguese and English.

title: Denmark  Did Not  Intervene  in  Foreign Exchange  Market in March--2nd Update
text:
(Revises first two paragraphs.)

By Charles Duxbury

Denmark's central bank said Tuesday that it refrained from intervening in the foreign exchange market in March, in a sign that the Danish currency has stabilized against the euro following weeks of volatility brought on by the European Central Bank's stimulus efforts.

The Danish central bank has been battling to stabilize the exchange rate, its core task, since the ECB announced a massive bond-buying stimulus program in January and sent the euro plummeting against other currencies, including the krone.

Nationalbanken said its foreign-exchange reserves remained at an elevated 737.1 billion kroner ($107.2 billion) after it sold a record amount of its own currency in January and February to weaken it but that it had stayed out of the foreign exchange market last month.

The central bank has been battling to stabilize the exchange rate, its core task, since the ECB kicked off a massive bond-buying stimulus program earlier this year and sent the euro plummeting against other currencies, including the krone.

As well as selling kroner, Denmark cut interest rates four times earlier this year and suspended bond issuance to sap interest in the krone among investors seeking better returns than they could get in the eurozone.

That interest rose sharply after Switzerland abandoned its currency ceiling to the euro as the ECB bond program loomed and traders began wondering if Denmark could be next.

The Danish central bank's only policy aim is to keep the euro's exchange rate within 2.25% above or below 7.46038 kroner to keep a lid on inflation and provide stability for domestic businesses that look to the eurozone as an important export market. It has no inflation target.

The peg has existed in close to its current form for more than three decades, first relative to the German currency and later against the euro.

Central bank Governor Lars Rohde has described the peg as the cornerstone of Danish economic policy and said the bank will do whatever it takes to defend it.

The ceasing of kroner sales in March is the latest sign that Nationalbanken's efforts have worked. Last Monday it issued short-term debt for the first time in two months.

title: GLOBAL CENTRAL BANKS: Denmark May See Krone's Tumult Fade
text:
Denmark's central bank has been under huge pressure to defend the currency peg to the euro, its main policy aim, but recent signs are that the storm could be passing.

In its most recent statement on its market activities, the central bank said it didn't intervene in currency markets in the latter part of February after buying record amounts of foreign exchange in January and early February to sap demand for the Danish krone.

The central bank's main policy goal is to keep the euro's exchange rate within 2.25% above or below 7.46038 kroner to keep a lid on inflation and provide stability for domestic businesses that rely on the eurozone as a market.

That task was made harder earlier this year by Switzerland's move to abandon its exchange-rate cap which got investors wondering whether Denmark could be next. Investors began buying up krone assets, pushing up its value, knowing that if the peg broke those assets would be worth more in euro terms.

The European Central Bank's bond-buying plan has also pushed down the value of the euro against the krone, forcing Denmark to cut interest rates four times and intervene extensively in currency markets to weaken its own currency.

With ECB asset-buying set to run for a protracted period, the Danish central bank will be on alert for moves higher in the krone's value compared with the euro.

If the current period of calmer currency markets continues, analysts expect Nationalbanken to keep rates unchanged for a period before gradually raising the deposit rate back toward zero.

However, if the krone starts strengthening again, Nationalbanken has made clear it is ready to intervene in currency markets and cut interest rates as necessary to maintain the peg.

"We are able and we are willing to do whatever it takes to defend the peg," Gov. Lars Rohde said recently. "The peg is the cornerstone of economic policy in Denmark and has very broad based support."
