title: EU SUMMIT: Nordic Caution Turns Into Skepticism About EU
text:
BRUSSELS (Dow Jones)--Europe's northern success stories always have been cautious about European unity. Now, though, they're becoming downright skeptical.

The skepticism goes far beyond frustration over the bogged-down referendum campaign for a proposed European Union constitution. They feel marginalized in an expanded bloc of 25 countries and disagree with the direction of the E.U.'s spending on agriculture and poor regions. At the same time, with the euro-zone economy sagging, Sweden, Finland and Denmark are busy lowering their own growth forecasts.

"We don't have time for grandiose visions of Europe," Finnish Foreign Minister Erkki Tuomioja told Dow Jones Newswires during a two-day summit of E.U. leaders here. "A pragmatic approach is required."

The Nordics traditionally have been at the fringe of E.U. affairs. None entered at the inception of the Union. Denmark joined in 1973, while Sweden and Finland only entered the E.U. in 1995. Norwegians have voted down membership twice and remain outside the E.U. Only Finland uses the euro; Denmark and Sweden have rejected it.

And while the three Nordic E.U. member countries have strong welfare states, they are as uncomfortable with French dirigisme as they are with British lassez faire.

The most immediate consequence will come with the much-maligned constitution. Opposition to the document, always strong, has soared in recent weeks following French and Dutch No votes.

Both Denmark and Sweden said Thursday that they will postpone planned referendums on the constitution. Sweden's Prime Minister Goran Persson said it would be impossible to go to voters if France and the Netherlands refuse to vote anew.

Danish Prime Minister Anders Fogh Rasmussen agreed, saying: "We can't put the treaty to a vote in Denmark if there's no treaty to vote on."

Even Tuomioja was skeptical about whether his country would go ahead with the much less sensitive parliamentary ratification, scheduled for August.

Yet the rest of the E.U.'s leaders at the summit rejected the Nordic request for a full-scale suspension. Instead, they said countries that want to proceed with a vote will be allowed to do so and that the issue will be revisited at another summit in June 2006. That could just postpone tensions: Nordic fervor for a failed constitution looks unlikely to improve in the meantime.

"When we see these leaders upstairs behind closed doors debating our future, it makes us uncomfortable," said Jens-Peter Bonde, a leading euro skeptic and Danish member of the European parliament. "The whole thing should be buried." 


 
       Budget, Enlargement Weigh On Nordic Minds 
   

Another concern is how Europe spends its money. Other E.U. leaders were demanding further cuts to the spending plans for 2007-2013 and lower individual contributions. The Scandinavians, meanwhile, want more money to be spent on research and development and less on agriculture and assistance for poor regions.

"We want a much more future-oriented budget" devoted "to research and development, innovation and education," Denmark's Rasmussen said Friday. "We should do our utmost to make the E.U. the most competitive economy in the world."

The Nordic opinion, particularly Sweden's, is key. They want big cuts in their contributions and they would like to see spending in 2007-2013 capped at 1% of the E.U.'s annual gross domestic product.

It's important politically to Sweden's Persson, who has seen support back home melting away, in large part because opposition voices criticize an E.U. budget. "We don't like the old E.U. politics of providing a lot of farm subsidies, etc.," said Lars Lindberg, the Europe spokesman for Sweden's opposition Moderaterna party.

If the budget talks break down later Friday, Swedish intransigence could be key. Persson said Friday he prefers "to take a year more than to get a bad decision."

The governments of the Nordic countries, agreed Finland's Tuomioja, "believe they can get a better deal by holding out."

In foreign policy, too, the E.U.'s divisions could have dangerous consequences. Tuomioja worries that his giant neighbor Russia will take advantage of that disarray to "press for advantages" in its negotiations over issues ranging from energy shipments to visa wavers.

A more specific foreign-policy concern of the Nordic countries is E.U. enlargement, which they fear will bring in a wave of cheap labor. Swedish labor unions are already blocking the use of Polish and Baltic construction workers on Swedish building projects.

The Nordic countries also fear the impact of the low taxes levied in eastern Europe. They want the E.U. to set minimum levels of VAT and income tax, so that Scandinavia's costly but popular welfare programs won't be put in jeopardy.

The E.U.'s present enlargement commissioner, Olli Rehn of Finland, admitted Thursday that the constitutional crisis has generated "enlargement blues," though he insisted "we are not taking any sabbatical from our work." In practical terms, that means Bulgaria and Romania, already accepted, will get in, but other potential applicants such as Croatia, Serbia and above all, Ukraine and Turkey, will have to wait.

Much depends on the economy. Like many others, Danish MEP Bonde believes that the troubled Constitution would have sailed through "if unemployment in France was 5%, not 11%." The Nordics don't face this problem - their economies are robust.

Yet weakness in the core of Western Europe hurts them, too. The Swedish government recently dropped its annual forecast for growth this year to 3% from 3.2%. In Finland, feeble demand from Europe coupled with a forestry strike has forced the government to pare back growth estimates to 2.5% from 3.0%, and it may have to do so again by next month.

Denmark is intervening in currency markets to support the Danish krone's peg with the collapsing euro, bloating its foreign currency reserves. The Norwegians are even more miffed, worried that their rising currency will take their exporters out of the marketplace as their central bank tightens rates to rein in growth.

The "economic and political turmoil we now see in continental Europe is slowing us down," Paer Nuder, the Swedish finance minister, recently told Dow Jones Newswires.

-By William Echikson, Dow Jones Newswires; 32-2-741-1482; william.echikson@dowjones.com

title: INTERVIEW-Danish crown needs steadying occasionally-c.bank.
text:
COPENHAGEN, Jan 27 (Reuters) - Euro outsider Denmark's central bank intervenes now and again in the currency market to fulfil its mission of keeping the crown stable against the euro, its governor said in a rare interview on Thursday.  

"Typically, we intervene to avoid abrupt movements in the exchange rate," said Bodil Nyboe Andersen, who steps down in October after more than 10 years in office.  

Along with Britain and neighbouring Sweden among the old members of the European Union, Denmark has opted not to join the single currency. But it has pegged its crown in a 2.25 percent band around a 7.46038 central rate against the euro.  

"We don't operate with a narrower band, but we keep it tight, typically slightly above the central rate," she said.  

Since the launch of the euro in 1999, the crown has traded between 7.4230 and 7.4670 per euro, or 0.5 percent on the stronger and 0.1 percent of the weaker side of the parity.  

Andersen said the bank buys or sells currency - often rather small amounts - to smooth out big capital flows which often stem from cross-border takeovers, local institutional investors' purchase of foreign securities or repatriation of funds and foreign investors' trading in Danish bonds and shares.  

"We tend to stabilise the market...it is easier to take it in the run-up than to step in at a later stage. It's a signal to the market that we are there if something big happens."  

The Danish central bank mirrors the European Central Bank's interest rate policy but on rare occasions moves independently.  

"If a development goes on over a long period and involves substantial amounts we will resort to changing the interest rate, typically by five basis points," she said.  

The spread between the bank's leading two-week rate and the ECB's refi-rate has been 15 basis points since June 2003.  

"History shows that even a five basis points cut could change the situation and stop an inflow for instance."  

Andersen said the crown's credibility was built up over the past 20 years and had left foreign exchange markets with a clear understanding of the Danish fixed exchange rate regime. The central rate has been unchanged since 1987, when it was fixed against the then German mark.  

Andersen noted that the crown's central rate was maintained through the general European Monetary System turmoil in the early 1990s and a more local currency crisis 1998, gaining a lot of credibility.  

"In fact we don't need to intervene very often because private banks do a lot of the stabilisation themselves, while still making a profit from it. That's fine, that's how the market should work."  

ADVICE TO ERM-2 NEWCOMERS  

Denmark joined the Exchange Rate Mechanism 2 (ERM-2) in 1999, when the single currency was launched. In June last year Estonia, Lithuania and Slovenia joined the club on their way to full euro membership.  

Andersen said new ERM-2 members should ensure their monetary policy only has one goal - to keep the currency stable.  

"You cannot take into consideration the domestic needs of the economy. You have to use interest rates only for stabilising the currency," she said.  

Denmark's central bank has no inflation or money supply target but adjusts rates and intervenes in the currency market for the sole purpose of keeping the crown stable.  

Danes rejected euro membership in a 2000 referendum, but Andersen is personally in favour of joining the euro.  

"When you already follow the rules of the game you could as well sit around the table," she said, adding that recent studies show that having the same currency promotes trading.  

"It's interesting to look into this because there could be an effect that we so far have overlooked in the debate about the effects of being an euro outsider," she said.  

Euro membership is not expected to become an issue ahead of Denmark's Feb. 8 general election. Polls show a majority of Danes want to swap their crown for the euro but a new referendum on the issue is not expected for the foreseeable future.

title: WRAPUP 1-Policymakers calm as euro surge gathers pace.
text:
BERLIN, Jan 6 (Reuters) - Euro zone policy makers said on Tuesday they were watching the speed of the euro's surge against the dollar but were not overly concerned at its current level, while German exporters remained bullish about prospects.  

The mild verbal intervention supported off-the-record comments by officials in recent days indicating the single currency's exchange rate would only become a problem if it reached $1.30.  

The currency was trading close to life highs just above $1.28 hit earlier on Tuesday around 1400 GMT.  

"It's true that brutal foreign exchange movements are bad for everyone but we have to refrain from any pessimism on this issue," French Budget Minister Alain Lambert told French radio, noting most French exports were within the euro zone.  

"For the moment, we're witnessing an evolution which still remains relatively reasonable," echoed Belgian Finance Minister Didier Reynders at a news conference in Brussels.  

"What is worrying are two things. Either too fast an evolution which we're not really witnessing today but could happen or an evolution which is in total contrast with the evolution of inflation and growth," Reynders added.  

The official insouciance contrasted with evidence the dollar's drop was beginning to cause strains in Europe.  

Dealers reported Denmark's central bank had intervened to keep its crown stable against the euro and Goldman Sachs cut its investment rating on European car makers, citing the currency's strength.  

"The euro has risen to a level that has severe implications for U.S. and UK earnings, and increases the competitive threat from Japan," Goldman Sachs analyst Keith Hayes said in a note cutting Germany's Volkswagen (VOWG.DE) to "underperform" and BMW (BMWG.DE) to "in-line".  

A rise in the euro's exchange rate makes it harder for European firms to win export orders and reduces the euro value of profits earned abroad. It also makes imports cheaper.  

A monthly index published by Germany's HWWA economic research institute showed the cost of euro zone commodity imports fell 5.0 percent year on year in euro terms in December despite a 14.6 percent rise in their dollar value.  

ECB RATES ON HOLD?  

Financial markets pushed back expectations of when the European Central Bank, which meets on Thursday, may hike interest rates from a record low of 2.0 percent.  

Euribor futures for March, a gauge of short-term euro zone interest rate expectations, rose to a three-month high at 97.920, implying three-month money market rates of 2.08 percent, and bond yields eased.  

"The move in the euro is raising expectations about steady rates," said HBOS economist Richard Batley.  

"Growth could be highly impacted by the strength of the euro and there is an idea that growth is highly geared towards the export sector at the moment."  

Strong exports helped pull Germany, the region's largest economy, out of recession in the third quarter. Data last week showed a two percent rise in exports helped the country to a record trade surplus of 135 billion euros in 2003.  

German exporters maintained on Tuesday an upbeat outlook despite a warning from a leading economic institute that the euro's rise was making firms less competitive on world markets.  

Anton Boerner, the head of Germany's BGA foreign and wholesale trade association, told Reuters he was optimistic exports could grow 4.5 percent this year despite the euro.  

"That (forecast) remains valid up until now," Boerner said.  

Boerner said he expected the euro to average between $1.250 and $1.275 this year, clearly above 2003 levels.  

"I don't see us reaching $1.40," Boerner said, adding however the currency could range as high as $1.30 or just over within the next three months.  

The DIW economic think tank said if the euro reached $1.30 it would be a problem for Germany's economy and at $1.35 the European Central Bank should cut rates.  

"Monetary policy makers must take responsibility for the recovery. They can't just keep their hands in their pockets and say it will come," DIW chief economist Gustav Adolf Horn said.  

However, a Reuters poll of 58 economists found 51 believed the next move in ECB rates would still be up, while seven expected a cut.

title: Danish cbank says stands ready to defend crown.
text:
COPENHAGEN, Dec 4 (Reuters) - Denmark's central bank, Nationalbanken, said on Wednesday it would intervene in the currency market and raise rates with determination if the Danish crown were to come under pressure. 

 It also said its monetary policy was shadowing that of the European Central Bank (ECB) but that it would adjust the difference between the ECB`s and its own leading lending rates according to the development in the currency reserves. 

 "When capital movements reverse at some point we are naturally ready to sell currency," central bank governer Bodil Nyboe Andersen said in the text of a speech prepared for delivery at the Danish Banks Association`s annual meeting. 

Currency inflow corresponding to almost 50 billion crowns and a strong crown against the euro has allowed the Danish central bank to gradually reduce the yield spread to ECB to 20 basis points in recent months. 

 "Those knowing us from earlier will have no doubts that the central bank`s defence of the crown will be utterly resolute in terms of intervention and widening of the interest rate spread." 

 Danes rejected euro membership in a referendum in September 2000. The central bank has no inflation or money supply target but adjusts rates for the sole purpose of keeping the crown stable against the euro. 

 "We are taking the crown`s rate against the euro and whether there has been a certain sustained flow of currency into consideration when adjusting the yield spread to ECB," Andersen said. 

 The crown is pegged to the euro  in a plus/minus 2.25 percent fluctuation band around a 7.46038 central parity in the ERM-2 grid. 

 At 1107 GMT, the crown stood around 7.4265 against the euro. 

 At end-November the Danish currency reserves were 195.9 billion crowns.

title: Denmark  to  intervene  if economy overheats - Jelved.
text:
COPENHAGEN, Aug 31 (Reuters) - The Danish government is ready to intervene and tighten fiscal policy at the first sign of any overheating of the economy caused by further European or Danish central bank rate cuts, Economy Minister Marianne Jelved said on Friday. 

 "If we see any sign of an overheating of the Danish economy as a result of further rate cuts by the European and Danish central banks, we will not hesitate to react with a tightening of fiscal policy, there can be no doubt about that," Jelved told Reuters. 

 Denmark`s central bank, Nationalbanken, on Thursday cut its key rates by 30 and 25 basis points respectively after the European Central Bank (ECB) cut its minimum bid rate earlier in the day. 

 The bank reduced its two-week certificates of deposit and lending rates to 4.65 percent from 4.95 percent, citing the ECB trimming and the current strength of the crown currency. 

 At the same time the Danish central bank reduced its less important key discount rate to 4.25 from 4.50 percent. 

 There are indications that further ECB rate cuts could be in the pipeline this autumn, which could cause problems for the Danish government's economic policy, sparking rises in consumption, wages and higher inflation. 

 "For the government the firm crown policy is of paramount importance. We are pledged to conduct tighter fiscal policy than that adopted in the euro zone and we will do so even if the need for intervention (to stop overheating of the economy) is needed on the eve of an election," she said. 

 The Danish crown is pegged to the euro in a plus/minus 2.25 percent fluctuation band around central parity of 7.46038 and the bank always follows ECB adjustments in interest rates. 

 Denmark is due to hold a general election by mid-March 2002 at the latest.

title: Danish c.bank indicates less need for  fx - intervention .
text:
COPENHAGEN, April 19 (Reuters) - Denmark`s central bank governor said on Thursday the Danish foreign exchange market was in "good balance", indicating a declining need for stabilising intervention. 

 "The recent months have shown that the market has become better to balance demand and supply," Bodil Nyboe Andersen told the Association of Danish Mortgage Banks` annual meeting. 

 "That has in some periods implied a little bigger daily price fluctuations (of the crown against the euro)," she said. 

 Last year the central bank, Nationalbanken, was very active in stabilising the crown against the single currency in order to avoid jitters connected to the country's September 28 euro membership referendum. 

 The Danish central bank has no inflation or money supply target but adjusts key rates for the sole purpose of keeping the crown stable against the euro. 

 The crown is pegged to the euro in a plus/minus 2.25 percent fluctuation band around central parity of 7.46038. But the central bank has said it aims at keeping the crown in a much narrower band, without giving further details. 

 Since the euro was launched January 1, 1999 the crown has traded within a tight 0.5 percent range. 

 Andersen also said a economic slowdown in Europe would not be too harmful to Denmark. 

 "The tight labour market puts a limit on how much the economy can grow without threatening the (current) economic balance," she said. 

 "Many businesses are close to their capacity limits and would therefore not suffer from slightly lower growth in demand."

title: Danish  central bank  raises key interest rates.
text:
COPENHAGEN, Sept 29 (Reuters) - Denmark`s central bank raised key interest rates by 50 basis points to 5.60 percent on Friday, reiterating its determination to defend the crown's fixed exchange rate against the euro after Thursday's bigger than expected referendum rejection of euro membership. 

 Danes voted 53.1 to 46.9 percent against joining the euro in a referendum on Thursday and the bank said there had been "certain pressure" on the crown recently, forcing it to intervene to support the currency. 

 "Denmark's fixed exchange rate policy will be continued after yesterday's referendum," the bank said in a statement. "To avoid uncertainty about the crown's exchange rate, the central bank's lending and certificates of deposit rates are being raised by 0.50 percentage points to 5.60 percent with effect from September 29," it said. 

 The central bank's discount and key deposit rates remained at 4.50 percent.

title: Dollar Slips Against Euro Despite Denmark's Vote, but Climbs Against Yen
text:
A WSJ.com News Roundup 

 NEW YORK -- The dollar declined against the euro Friday, as traders seemed unwilling to test central bankers' resolve to support the euro despite Denmark's vote against joining the 11-nation monetary union. 

 The dollar also weakened against the pound, but climbed to a one-month high against the yen following weaker-than-expected consumer-spending data out of Japan. 

 Late Friday, the euro was quoted at 88.30 U.S. cents, up from 87.77 U.S. cents late Thursday in New York. 

 The dollar traded at 108.15 yen, up from 107.65 yen late Thursday. The pound bought $1.4750, up from $1.4623 late Thursday. 

 The euro's gains came in the aftermath of the Danish voters' rejection Thursday of joining the euro. The vote had been largely perceived in the currency markets as a litmus test for the euro. And while the outcome wasn't unexpected, it added to a lack of confidence in the euro, which at its all-time low of 84.38 cents hit earlier this month, had lost 28% of its value against the dollar since its launch in January 1999. The currency has fallen even further against the yen. 

 However, on Friday the euro was anchored in a tight range around 88 U.S. cents overnight, and the move down to 87.50 U.S. cents just ahead of the New York open was attributed to flows related to reports that the U.K.'s Vodafone Group PLC was about to sell its Italian unit Infostrada SpA to Enel SpA and possibly France Telecom. 

Foreign-exchange traders were hesitant to push the euro lower, fearing that the European Central Bank, with or without help from other central banks, would move to support the euro if it fell too far, too fast. 

 Traders may test the euro's downside next week, said Lara Rhame, currency economist at Brown Brothers Harriman & Co. "The referendum's behind us now. The euro has lost any support on that front." 

 In light of Denmark's vote, the Danish central bank raised one of its two key interest rates to reaffirm its commitment to a fixed-exchange rate policy for the krone. The central bank raised its lending rate by a half percentage point to 5.6%, but it left its other key rate, the discount rate, unchanged at 4.5%. The krone has been pegged to the German mark since 1982, and when monetary union kicked off, the country linked the krone to the euro. The currency is permitted to vary only within a 2.25% range against the euro, though Denmark's central bank as a rule intervenes when the krone moves more than 0.5% against the common currency. 

 Separately, ratings agency Fitch IBCA Inc. affirmed its AA+ long-term foreign-currency rating for Denmark, but it replaced its positive outlook with a stable outlook. 

 The biggest movement overnight was in dollar/yen, following Japanese data that showed that personal income and spending remained weak. The dollar triggered stops early in New York to hit an intraday high of 108.47, its highest level since August 22. 

 Spending by Japanese wage earners in August was 332,633 yen ($3,093) on average, down 2.9% in real terms from a year earlier, suggesting the recovery in the corporate sector has yet to filter through to households. 

 The market largely ignored U.S. data showing a modest rise of 0.4% in personal income in August, with spending up 0.6%.

title: Crown firms, bond yields ease as Danes vote on euro.
text:
COPENHAGEN, Sept 28 (Reuters) - The Danish crown firmed and debt yields eased on Thursday as market players speculated that reaction would be limited even if the Danes vote against adopting the euro in Thursday's referendum. 

 The crown firmed slightly against the euro to 7.4611 at 0830 GMT from 7.4652 at Wednesday's close as opinion polls indicated a tight vote. Danish bond yields narrowed slightly, reducing their spread over European debt. 

 Economists and dealers attributed the moves not to confidence that Danes might vote 'yes', but to growing awareness that the market impact of a 'no' was likely to be limited. 

 "People aren't worried that much that a 'no' will cause that much currency turmoil," said Keld Holm, head of research at BG Bank in Copenhagen. 

 Holm predicted that the spread of Danish 10-year bonds over euro zone bonds would widen to 50 basis points if the Danes reject the euro, and narrow to about 20 if they accept it. 

 At 0830 GMT, the benchmark 10-year yield spread over German Bunds was 35 basis points, down from 38 late Wednesday. 

 Membership of the euro would tend to reduce the spread by lessening the currency risk of investing in Danish debt. The Danish crown has weakened slightly in recent weeks on fears that rejection could cause investors to pull funds out of Denmark. 

 But it has not tested the intervention limits of the 2.25 percent band in which the crown is locked against the euro. And markets appear to believe the Danish government's pledge to keep the crown inside that corridor if the Danes vote 'no'. 

 Danish stocks were little moved on Thursday with the top-20 KFX index 0.3 percent down. Dealers expect little impact on Danish equities whatever the result. 

 Exit polls will give initial indications of the outcome from about 1200 GMT and the final result will be known at around 2030 GMT. Markets are expected to tread water until the afternoon when the first polls could cause volatility. 

 Much will depend on how clear the first exit polls are, dealers said. 

 MAASTRICHT TREATY 

 If the 'yes' and 'no' camps are as close as opinion polls suggest, the outcome may still be completely open by the time Danish markets close and any reaction will not be felt until Friday. 

 Denmark's referendum on the Maastricht Treaty on European integration in 1992 was such a cliffhanger that the running vote count was indicating a 'yes' just 15 minutes before the final result showed Danes had in fact voted 'no'. 

 One dealer predicted the crown would drift lower in the course of the day and predicted it would move in a 7.4600-50 per euro range ahead of clear indications of the result. 

 "Even if the referendum were to be defeated we view Danish bonds as attractive on a fundamental basis," Merrill Lynch fixed income analysts said in a market commentary this week. 

 "Danish fiscal performance is significantly better and macroeconomic performance over the last five years has been better than the euro land average," it said. 

 The intervention available to support the crown was "formidable," the report added. "Speculators are likely to conclude fairly quickly that testing the central banks' resolve is a no-win proposition." 

 The vote, so close that just 20,000 to 30,000 Danes could determine the outcome, could have a greater impact on the euro. 

 The Danish verdict on the euro could initially lead to sharp swings in the single currency. But financial markets expect the European Central Bank to intervene to prop it up if a 'no' vote sparks heavy losses. 

 The euro was broadly supported on Thursday ahead of the referendum result and was quoted at $0.8840 euros at 0830 GMT. 

 Economists polled by Reuters said the outcome could have an impact of 3.5 U.S. cents - a 2.0 cent fall if the Danes reject it, and a 1.5 cent gain if they say yes. But opinions on the impact are divided. Some see the euro shrugging off the result.

title: FX  options market braces for Danish poll fallout.
text:
LONDON, Sept 27 (Reuters) - The currency options market is primed for sharp moves in the euro's exchange rate over the next few days amid concern that a looming Danish referendum could provide the trigger for central bank intervention. 

 If Denmark votes on Thursday against joining the single currency the euro is expected to suffer a further denting of sentiment, while a 'yes' vote would be supportive. 

 There is also the risk that central banks from the Group of Seven nations could intervene together to buy euros, as they did last week, and once again trigger a sharp spike up in the single currency. 

 There were even some fears that intervention could take place ahead of the referendum results, given that G7 intervention took financial markets by surprise on Friday ahead of the G7 finance ministers meeting. 

 "The market is really pricing in a big move and is trying to buy options for Friday, to get a two-way bet in," said an options trader at a European bank in London. 

 Implied volatility, which reflects expectations of how much prices will gyrate, was at 18.0/19.5 percent for one-week euro/dollar options, according to Reuters data , up more than one percentage point from Thursday. 

 "Even though vols are high, the risk/reward means that it is still better to be long the front end, because of any gapping risk in spot," said the London-based options dealer. 

 "Being short options and trying to lead stop-loss orders is just not going to work because spot has the potential to move so much that you are not going to be able to stop yourself out rapidly enough." 

 DANISH VOTE SEEN A CLOSE CALL 

 The latest opinion polls show that voting on whether Denmark joins the euro is likely to be close on Thursday. 

 While the market has mostly been pricing in a 'no' vote over the last week, this week's survey of the latest polls showed a rebalancing of the public's view. 

 "Implied volatilities at the front end are firm and reasonably well bid following Friday's joint intervention and with the possibility of further intervention and event risk coming from tomorrow's Danish referendum," said Paul Mackel, currency analyst at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson in Frankfurt. 

 "Spot has been slowly creeping up towards $0.89 because some people are expecting that there could be some intervention before the referendum." 

 The euro/dollar spot rate was within half a cent of its day's highs above $0.8880 , less than two cents away from Friday's post-intervention peaks above $0.90 and up more than five percent from record lows set last week. 

 Dealers said if the Danes rejected the single currency, the euro/dollar spot rate would trade lower and front-end vols would initially fall. 

 They said options buying in the middle of the curve would then come in, on the risk that the euro would fall to new lows. 

 But analysts said wariness of further central bank intervention to support the euro could limit losses in the euro/dollar spot rate. 

 "A 'no' in Denmark is more or less priced into the market because euro sentiment has been negative for a while now," said an options trader at a bank in Europe. 

 "But if we saw intervention combined with a 'yes' in Denmark, it would obviously have a considerable impact - more than if we had intervention with a 'no'."

title: Danish crown spirits seen lifted by G7 euro rescue.
text:
LONDON, Sept 25 (Reuters) - The Danish crown sailed up to three-week peaks against the euro on Monday with a tailwind from last week's joint G7 intervention on the euro as dealers bet such action could help erode Danish opposition to euro entry. 

 Opinion polls released after Friday's G7 rescue operation in favour of the sinking euro suggested pro-euro Danes might be clawing back ground against their opponents although the outcome of euro referendum on September 28 remained a tough call. 

 While several major currencies tumbled against the euro after the joint intervention, the Danish crown staged an impressive rally against the single currency, firming to its highest level since the beginning of September. 

 Analysts said intervention and a joint euro-supportive statement by the Group of Seven at the weekend were powerful signs of international committment to halting the euro's slide. 

 This could help rebalance the view on the euro's fortunes among some Danes, whose negative feelings toward the currency had been exacerbated by its past weakness, they added. 

 "The strengthening of the crown might be indirectly linked to intervention, but through the opinion polls rather than through intervention in itself," said Carsten Valgreen, head of macroeconomic research at BG Bank in Copenhagen. 

 "Intervention was on the front page of every newspaper in Denmark. One of the things which drew the polls towards the 'No' in the past few weeks was the euro's weakening. But if intervention works, it will strengthten the 'Yes' side and that would help the crown." 

 The crown appreciated as far as 7.4570 crowns per euro on Monday, moving back to the strong side of its 7.46038 central parity against the single currency. 

 REFERENDUM OUTCOME STILL A RIDDLE 

 Analysts said the Danish crown was benefitting from speculation that the chances of a 'Yes' vote might be improving, even though the result was far from clear as opinion polls in Denmark still appeared to be mixed just days before the referendum. 

 On Sunday a daily Vilstrup poll found the pro-euro camp in the lead for the first time since September 12 and Megafon's latest television survey on Monday said the 'No' side lead had shrunk by three points to 50-42 percent. 

 A Gallup poll said however the leadership of the euro opponents had widened to four points from three. 

 "The outlook for the referendum is more balanced. And perhaps people feel that intervention will actually help the (yes) vote in Denmark," said Stephanie Pfeiffer senior European economist at Deutsche Bank in London. 

 Analysts said a 'Yes' vote would attract international capital into Danish assets after month of uncertainty and thus help the Danish crown. 

 But they also feared the Danish population was not fully aware of the economic consequences of voting one way or another, such as the risk that the Danish central bank could raise interest rates sharply to defend the crown in case of a rejection of euro membership. 

 "The crown is getting some joy from the fact the polls have improved (for the 'Yes' side), even though it's a slight improvement," said Julie Collins Thompson, market economist at BNP Paribas in London. 

 "But you still have a high percentage of undecided voters and in past referendums they had tended to vote 'No'."

title: CORRECTED - UPDATE 1-Danish euro 'no' lead dwindles.
text:
In COPENHAGEN story "UPDATE 1-Danish euro 'no' lead 

  dwindles in new polls please read in 5th para: "...from 

  7.4590..." instead of "...from 7.5690..." (correcting Danish 

 crown's close against euro in Copenhagen). 

 A corrected repetition follows. 

 By Peter Starck 

 COPENHAGEN, Sept 22 (Reuters) - Euro opponents in Denmark were in retreat but clung to their lead over supporters in two fresh opinion polls Friday, six days before the Danes vote in a referendum on whether or not to adopt the EU single currency. 

 The latest survey by Gallup, whose daily polls have registered a successively tighter lead for the anti-euro 'no' side since September 19, saw opponents score 47 percent, down from 48 percent Thursday, while the pro-euro 'yes' camp advanced one point to 41 percent. 

 A new Vilstrup survey found 45 percent saying 'no', while 41 percent said 'yes' - a sharp shift from Thursday's poll, which saw euro rejectionists 10 points ahead by 48-38 percent. Vilstrup had seen the 'no' side's lead growing daily since Monday. 

 The statistical error margin is some three percentage points in both polls. Since the two research institutes began releasing daily polls in early September, trend shifts recorded by Gallup have been echoed by Vilstrup with a time lag of about three days. 

 The Danish crown, which is pegged to the euro in a plus/minus 2.25 percent fluctuation band, strengthened to 7.4582 in late U.S. trading from 7.4590 at the 1500 GMT Copenhagen close. 

 During the European trading day, the crown firmed for the second consecutive session, breaking back onto the stronger side of its central parity for the first time since September 12. 

 The euro hurtled up more than five percent against the dollar early Friday as central banks from Europe, the United States and Japan united in a concerted intervention to buy euros, pushing the currency temporarily above 90 U.S. cents. 

 But the euro pared much of those gains, falling below 88 cents in early U.S. afternoon trade in the absence of further central bank buying. 

 A snap Reuters poll of economists in North America and Europe forecast the euro would be at 89 cents a month from now. 

 The beleaguered currency has shed more than 25 percent of its value against the dollar over the past 20 months, falling to a record low near 84.40 cents Wednesday after being launched with fanfare at $1.17 in Jan. 1999. 

 EURO FALL HURT DANISH 'YES' 

 The euro's steep fall was mentioned by half of Danish voters in a recent poll as a key factor influencing their views in the run-up to the referendum. A widening lead for the 'no' side coincided with the latest bout of euro weakness that began in September. 

 Leading 'yes and 'no' campaigners in Denmark said Friday any euro rebound sparked by intervention would hardly swing opinions again. 

 "I doubt ... that the exchange rate of the euro will have direct effect on the outcome of the election," Denmark's staunchly pro-euro Prime Minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen told Reuters Television, referring to the September 28 plebiscite. 

 "We have passed that period where the euro's exchange rate plays a dominant role in people's mind." 

 Holger Nielsen, leader of the far-left Socialist People's Party and one of Denmark's most vociferous anti-euro campaigners, agreed. 

 "Danes know very well that the euro is a very weak and unstable currency, so the intervention will have no significance for voters when they go to the ballot box next Thursday," he told Reuters, adding: "The majority is going to vote 'no' to the euro." 

 Rasmussen dismissed the notion his campaign was a lost cause. 

 "Nothing is sure right now. It will be close," he told a news conference before the latest Gallup and Vilstrup polls had been published. 

 Finance Minister Mogens Lykketoft, who also thinks Denmark should join the single currency, said the European Central Bank's reasoning for the intervention - concern about the potential implications of recent moves in the euro - showed that the 'no' campaigners' attempts to frighten Danes to vote 'no' by portraying the euro as a weak currency were groundless. 

 "The big powers think that the euro is an undervalued currency and that this hampers U.S. and Japanese exports," Lykketoft told Danish TV2 television news.

title: INTERVIEW-Danish economy minister confident of euro "Yes".
text:
COPENHAGEN, Sept 20 (Reuters) - Denmark's Economy Minister said she was confident Danes would vote to adopt the euro in next week's referendum, despite a lead for the "No" campaign in recent opinion polls. 

 "I believe in a 'Yes' - that's what I am fighting for," Marianne Jelved told Reuters in an interview on Wednesday. 

 "It's clear that some of the polls show an unpleasant picture, but it's a picture that I cannot recognise when I meet people at rallies or in taxis," she said. 

 Recent opinion polls ahead of the September 28 referendum have given the anti-euro campaign a lead of up to 11 points. But the polls suggest that up to 25 percent of Denmark's four million voters have still not decided which way to vote. 

 It is among these wavering Danes that the strongly pro-euro minister said she saw hope. 

 "My experience is that when I get the opportunity to answer people's questions they change their minds. It's positive that information and dialogue works," Jelved said. 

 If Danes reject swapping their crown for the European Union's single currency it will only have a limited affect on the Danish crown and bond yield spreads over the euro zone, she said. 

 "The financial markets have already discounted a 'No' although the crown could come under some pressure," she said. 

 "But this will be nothing that we cannot handle. We have great experience in tackling pressure against the crown." 

Denmark's central bank, Nationalbanken, was last seen intervening in the foreign exchange market to support the crown on Monday, when the currency hit a record low against the euro of 7.4690. 

 DENMARK TO KEEP RATE POLICY IF "NO" VOTE WINS 

 Jelved stressed that in the event of a "No" vote, Denmark would stick to the stable exchange rate policy that has been the cornerstone of Danish monetary policy for almost two decades. 

 If the crown comes under heavy fire from foreign investors who hold some 350 billion crowns worth of Danish bonds, Denmark would defend the currency within the crown's current peg to the euro and not widen the fluctuation band - as happened during the EMS-crisis in 1993. 

 "A fluctuation band of plus/minus 15 percent is totally uninteresting for Denmark. Otherwise we would not have fought for a 2.25 percent fluctuation band," she said. 

 Denmark was allotted a 2.25 percent fluctuation band around its central parity against the euro at 7.46038 in September 1998 by its partners in the so-called ERM-2 grid. 

 Although Jelved was confident that the central bank could handle any pressure on the crown with the normal tools of intervention and higher interest rates, she said Denmark would be more vulnerable if an outright majority of Danes voted "No". 

 "In the event of a new Asia crisis like we saw in the autumn of 1998, Denmark would be more vulnerable as we can no longer take shelter from the market perception that Denmark sooner or later would join the euro," she explained. 

 "The fact that we say 'No' in a referendum to the euro makes us more vulnerable, she said, adding that any future referendum could take quite a long time. 

 Euro opponents in Denmark turned the tables on supporters earlier this month after the euro's latest bout of weakness set in. Analysts say the euro's collapse and the shift in voter sentiment in Denmark are feeding on each other. 

 Jelved declined to comment on the impact of the euro's slide on the Danish referendum. 

 "Don't ask me. It's not my currency," the minister responsible for the Danish crown currency said.

title: UPDATE 1-Anti-euro Danes stay ahead in new polls.
text:
COPENHAGEN, Sept 19 (Reuters) - Danes averse to signing up for the European Union's euro single currency stayed comfortably ahead of opponents in two opinion polls published on Tuesday. 

 On September 28, Denmark will hold a referendum on whether to join the euro, which has lost almost 28 percent in value against the dollar since its launch in January 1999. 

 A Danish 'no' vote could deal a blow to the already groggy euro, which hit yet another record-low against the dollar on Tuesday, as well as dim the outlook for fellow outsiders Britain and Sweden signing up any time soon and possibly complicate so-called enlargement talks about opening the EU's doors for up to a dozen new member states, mainly from Eastern Europe. 

 The latest daily Gallup poll gave the anti-euro 'no' side 49 percent, unchanged from Monday, while the pro-euro 'yes' camp edged one point up to 38 percent, national DR1 television's text-TV news said. The rest, 13 percent, were undecided. 

 A daily Vilstrup survey gave opponents 45 percent compared with 42 percent for supporters, the daily newspaper Politiken said on its Internet Web site. Vilstrup also found 13 percent undecided. In the previous Vilstrup survey published on Monday opponents led supporters by 44-42 percent. 

 Both polls' margin of error is three percentage points. 

 Earlier on Tuesday, analysts said Denmark's europhile political establishment had begun preparing for defeat in the euro referendum, which Prime Minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen has described as Denmark's most important foreign policy decision since Danes voted in 1972 to join the then European Community. 

 "The 'yes' side is growing increasingly desperate and people are already preparing to 'wash their hands' in case of defeat," Danske Bank, Denmark's biggest financial group, said in a daily report. 

 EU CRISIS 

 A Danish 'no' to the euro could heighten a sense of crisis in the European Union, already reeling from its battered currency, widespread tax revolts and unease over a heavy-handed policy towards Austria, analysts say. 

 Popular support for the EU could sink to new lows, triggering a fresh sell-off of the euro, which retreated to new lifetime lows against major currencies as supportive words from a host of top European officials proved no match for bearish market sentiment. 

 Europe's beleaguered single currency sank to fresh record lows against the dollar in early U.S. trade, as words of concern about the euro from French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin and his Italian counterpart Guiliano Amato, failed to lend it much support. 

 "As soon as some guys out of Europe start speaking about the weak euro everyone just starts selling," said Jan Souleyman, senior yen trader at Credit Agricole Indosuez. 

 "Talk is cheap, if they want to get their currency stronger then they are going to have to act," he added. 

 The euro slid a new low of 84.77 cents in U.S. trading, having slumped below 85 cents and below 91 yen to fresh records against the Japanese currency in Asian trade. 

 Euro opponents in Denmark turned the tables on supporters earlier this month after the euro's latest bout of weakness set in on September 6. Analysts say the euro's collapse and the shift in voter sentiment in Denmark are feeding on each other. 

 Analysts said only coordinated intervention between the European Central Bank, the Bank of Japan and the U.S. Federal Reserve would have a lasting effect on the euro.

title: Danish  central bank  bought crowns for euro-dealers.
text:
LONDON, Sept 15 (Reuters) - Denmark's central bank, Nationalbanken, intervened on the foreign exchanges on Friday, buying crowns for euros, European dealers said. 

 Nationalbanken reportedly bought crowns when its currency hit 7.4675 per euro earlier on Friday. That was the Danish crown's lowest level since the euro was launched on January 1, 1999. 

 This was at least the second time this week that the central bank has been spotted intervening in the market. 

 Its intervention comes even though the crown remains well inside its allotted 2.25 percent fluctuation band around its central parity against the euro at 7.46038. 

Intervention volumes were moderate and the impact on market sentiment was undramatic, one dealer said. 

 Analysts attribute the crown's fall to record lows against the euro to Danish euro opponents' widening lead over supporters in fresh opinion polls ahead of Denmark's September 28 referendum on whether to join the euro.

title: Danish  forex  market makers to widen EUR/DKK spread.
text:
COPENHAGEN, Sept 15 (Reuters) - Market makers in the Danish forex market have decided to widen the bid and ask spread for interbank euro quotes against the Danish crown , chief dealer Tom Pietraszek at Unibank Markets said on Friday. 

 The move is to secure an efficient market amid greater volatility ahead of the country's knife-edge September 28 referendum on whether to join the euro. 

 Market makers also agreed to widen the spread even further when trading resumes on September 29, the day after the vote, he told Reuters by telephone. 

 "We (market makers) have decided to widen the spread marginally with effect from (next) Monday," Pietraszek told Reuters. 

 "We want to retain a sensible and liquid market in order to service our clients," he explained. 

 As of Monday, September 18, market makers in Copenhagen will quote EUR/DKK with a spread of five points (i.e. 7.4670/75) for amounts up to 20 million euros, up from three points (i.e. 7.4670/73) under the current market-maker agreement, said another currency dealer, who asked not to be named. 

 "On the 29th we expect higher volatility than normally in the exchange rate," Pietraszek said. 

 "It is therefore likely that we start up with a somewhat wider spread. (It would be) widest in the event of a 'No'." 

 Earlier on Friday, Denmark's central bank, Nationalbanken, intervened in the foreign exchange market, buying crowns for euros, European dealers said. 

 Nationalbanken reportedly bought crowns at 7.4675 per euro, its lowest level since the single currency was launched on January 1, 1999. 

 Analysts attributed the crown's fall to record lows against the euro to Danish euro opponents' widening lead over supporters in the latest opinion polls. 

 With almost one-fifth of voters undecided, analysts say the outcome is too close to call.

title: UPDATE 1-Danish cenbank  intervenes  to support crown.
text:
COPENHAGEN, Sept 13 (Reuters) - Denmark's central bank intervened in the foreign exchange market in early trade on Wednesday, selling euros to support the weakening crown , dealers said. 

 The central bank, Nationalbanken, bought crowns at around 7.4660 per euro, a foreign exchange dealer at a big Nordic commercial bank told Reuters. Intervention volumes were moderate. 

 "It is not a heavy intervention but it is a signal," one dealer said. 

 A central bank spokeswoman declined to comment, citing standard Nationalbanken policy of never talking in public about its daily foreign exchange market operations. 

 The Danish currency softened in morning trade to near its life-low of 7.4667 against the euro set on June 8. The crown remained well inside its allotted plus/minus 2.25 percent fluctuation range in the ERM-2 currency grid. The crown's ERM-2 central parity is 7.46038. 

 Nationalbanken's policy is to intervene in the market to smooth excessive intra-day volatility that could be interpreted as going against Denmark's long-standing commitment to exchange rate stability. 

 At 0855 GMT, the crown stood at 7.4645 per euro. 

 Analysts and dealers attribute the crown's weakening to fresh opinion polls suggesting that Danes opposed to euro membership are pulling ahead of supporters two weeks before Denmark's September 28 referendum on whether to join the euro. 

 The implied volatility in the crown-euro cross jumped to 1.2-1.7 on Wednesday from 0.9-1.4 on Tuesday. The ratio is a measure of market expectations of future swings and a higher reading implies greater uncertainty. 

 The benchmark forward rate agreement (FRA), three-month IMM December, shot up to 6.12/16 percent from 6.07/15 late on Tuesday. 

 A daily Gallup opinion poll gave euro opponents a five-point lead over supporters for the third day running and a daily Vilstrup survey showed the anti-euro "No" side pulling even with the pro-euro "Yes" camp. .

title: POLL-Crown's euro peg to hold even if Danes say no to EMU.
text:
LONDON, Aug 18 (Reuters) - The Danish currency will stay hitched to the euro even if Danes vote "no" to joining European monetary union in a referendum next month, economists say. 

 According to the median forecast of 35 economists surveyed by Reuters, there is an 85 percent chance that the crown's peg to the euro will hold for at least 12 months if Danes reject the common currency in the September 28 vote. 

 "The Danes love the link," said Jens Peter Neergard of Den Danske Bank in Copenhagen. For nearly two decades, the crown has been wedded to the German mark or euro even though Denmark opted out of the single currency's launch last year. 

 At the moment the referendum is too close to call with opinion polls showing the "yes" and "no" forces running neck and neck. 

 But there is strong support across the political spectrum for maintaining the euro peg in event of a "no" vote. 

 "No politician has advocated Denmark giving up its policy of exchange rate stability between the Danish crown and the euro," said Niels Christensen at Societe Generale in Paris. 

 The pledges of Danish authorities and, more significantly, the powerful European Central Bank to defend the link even if Denmark stays out of EMU should deter speculators from trying to drive down the crown , economists said. 

 WHO WANTS TO TAKE ON ECB? 

 "Why would you want to bet against the ECB? I don't think there's an appetite to speculate against the crown," said Christel Aranda-Hassel at CSFB in London. 

 ECB president Wim Duisenberg pledged in July that the ECB "will do everything in its power" to keep Denmark in ERM-2, which is the waiting room for would-be EMU members." 

 At its request, Denmark has a narrow 2.25 percent deviation band around its central rate of 7.46 per euro, not the standard 15 percent band that applies to Greece, the other ERM-2 member. 

 Having made 'appropriate use' of its own foreign reserve holdings, countries can draw on a three-month financing facility at the ECB which should in principle be automatically available and unlimited, said Holger Schmieding of Merrill Lynch. 

 While the ECB is under no formal obligation to lend indefinite support, "the ECB is unlikely to let Denmark down", said Schmieding. "A Danish devaluation, a widening of the bands or a forced exit of Denmark from the ERM2 would be probably seen as a defeat for the ECB and a further blow to the bank's reputation - an outcome the ECB will probably want to avoid." 

Currency speculators made vast profits when they forced the British pound's exit from the original exchange rate mechanism in 1992. Already, the Danish crown has come under pressure because of some polls favouring a "no" vote and the National Bank has intervened to support the currency. 

 RAISE RATES? 

Denmark's first line of defence against a currency attack might be to raise interest rates modestly, economists said. Speculators could possibly overcome any resistance by the Danish national bank whose reserves have been falling in recent months. 

 "But a clear sign the big ECB will let Denmark draw on an unlimited credit line...should drive the speculators away," Schmieding said. 

 Economists added Danish M2 money supply represents just 1.7 percent of the Euro zone total so ECB support for the crown would only have a negligible effect on Euroland money supply. 

 Still, not all economists are so certain the link would hold. "Under a "no" scenario, Denmark would be the country with the largest reservations toward the euro and a formal link to the euro," said Teis Knuthsen of SEB Merchant Banking. 

 "A currency crisis will occur at the point where the Danish economy warrants an easier economic policy and the euro zone is tightening. A fixed exchange rate system is not sustainable if there is no planned convergence," he said.

title: Little Relief Likely For Danish Krone Ahead Of Euro Vote
text:
COPENHAGEN -(Dow Jones)- These are turbulent days for the Danish krone, with the outcome of the referendum over Danish euro membership in the balance and some economists predicting sharp currency depreciation against the euro. 

 "Pressure on the Danish currency will intensify" as the Sept. 28 referendum comes closer, predicted Steve Barrow, currency strategist with Bear Stearns in London. 

 "The Danish central bank may be forced to accept a move up to DKK7.50 to the euro by the time of the referendum." 

 A rejection of the euro by Danish voters could send the euro as high as DKK7.60, according to Barrow. 

 However, some investors may wonder why there's all this fuss. Tuesday, the euro was trading around DKK7.4643, still firmly within the band set under the European exchange rate mechanism. Under the ERM II agreement, the Danish currency can fluctuate by 2.25% on either side of a central parity of DKK7.46038 to the euro. 

 And since the beginning of the year, when the krone was stronger than its parity rate, it has depreciated by a modest 0.3%. Even if the krone were to weaken to DKK7.50 or DKK7.60 to the euro, it would still be inside the official band. 

 However, analysts say that for the usually rock-steady Danish currency, such a depreciation would be a big thing. 

 "The de facto band inside which the krone fluctuates is far narrower than the official one. Since the ERM II came into force, the fluctuations on either side of the parity rate have been below 0.5%," said Johnny Petersen, an economist with Jyske Bank, a Danish regional bank. 

 Indeed, growing doubts over the referendum's outcome threatens to widen the trading band within the trading band. A slew of recent opinion polls have shown gains for the "no" camp. An influential monthly poll, released last week by Danish business daily newspaper Boersen, puts the "no" side ahead of the "yes" vote by 50% to 43%. 

 That has intensified pressure on the krone, a process reflected in money market rates. 

 "We are seeing quite significant pressure building up in the forward rate agreements," Barrow of Bear Stearns noted. 


   Krone Likely To Stay Within 2.25% Band



In spite of the increased volatility and uncertainty, most economists
expect the 2.25% band to remain intact, even if the krone is trading
with wider swings within it.



"In recent weeks the likelihood of the krone remaining inside its
official band has grown considerably," said Jyske Bank's Petersen.



The krone found some support from European Central Bank President Wim
Duisenberg, who last week reiterated that the ECB remains committed to
defending the Danish krone, even in the case of a no vote. Under the
bilateral agreement between Denmark and the ECB, the ECB is obliged to
intervene to support the krone if the currency were to move out of its
band.



"What we might see is a sliding process, where the shock effect of a
'no' is gradually being priced in," Petersen said.



The nervous krone situation is already taking its toll on the Danish
central bank's war chest.



Danish foreign reserves dropped DKK9.9 billion in June to a total
DKK122.8 billion. During the first half of the year, reserves decreased
DKK42.5 billion, or 26%.



However, not all of that was spent defending the krone. Up to half the
decline is attributable to the government's repayment of foreign credits
and investors shifting out of Danish assets into international
technology stocks early in the year, economists say.



Nevertheless, some market players believe the Danish central bank may
have to resort to rate hikes, if pressure on the krone continues in the
run-up to the referendum.



"The Danish central bank can find itself in a position where it has to
press up interest rates quite aggressively," Barrow said.



Denmark's benchmark lending rate currently stands at 4.70%, 45 basis
points above the ECB refinancing rate.

title: Swedish crown seen at risk if Danes snub euro.
text:
LONDON, June 16 (Reuters) - A Danish rejection of euro entry in a referendum this autumn would have a spillover effect on neighbouring Sweden to the point of hurting the Swedish crown, analysts said on Friday. 

 Waning support among Danes for euro membership has already started to dent the Danish crown's value against the single currency, forcing Denmark's central bank to intervene on the foreign exchange markets to defend its currency on June 2. 

 Such scepticism could claim a second victim - the Swedish crown - if investors start thinking that a Danish 'No' to the euro could jeopardise Sweden's expected bid to join the euro. 

 "If Denmark gives a resounding 'No', it would make it very difficult for the Swedish government to sell the idea of joining the euro to the people and the Swedish crown could come under some speculative attack," said Danny Gabay, economist at JP Morgan in London. 

 "We could therefore see some selling of Swedish crowns." 

 The Swedish crown was trading around 8.25 against the euro on Friday, up about 14 percent since the euro's launch in January 1999. 

 "There will be some spillover effect (from the Danish vote)," said Steve Barrow, currency strategist at Bear Stearns. He expects the Swedish crown to be trading around 8.40 in three months time. 

 EURO FOCUS TO HEAT UP NORDIC SUMMER 

 Financial markets in Sweden and Denmark, which conduct less than 10 percent of their trade with each other, are expected to become increasingly focused on the euro debate in the run-up to the Danish vote on September 28. 

 More than the economic ties, the psychological link could play a big role in influencing sentiment in the two Nordic countries given the public has so far snubbed their leaders' eagerness to join the euro in both countries. Only last week, Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson said a rejection of the euro in Denmark would have a great impact on Swedish public opinion. 

 A Danish 'No' is expected to weaken Swedish euro support and weaken the crown from its current level, which analysts said was pricing in the view that Sweden would join the euro zone, towards which it directs more than 40 percent of its exports. 

 "There probably is going to be a knock-on effect because of the proximity of the two countries and the economic ties they share," said Juli Collins-Thompson, EMU-outs market economist at BNP Paribas Group in London. 

 "If there is a 'No' vote in Denmark people will think that this can delay Sweden entry. If there is a selling of Swedish assets, there will be some feedthrough effect on the currency." 

 In March this year Sweden's ruling Social Democrats voted in favour of joining the euro, but a decision will be taken at a referendum that is not expected before autumn 2002. 

 But the latest survey by the Swedish Statistics Office on Wednesday showed that opposition to the euro rose by seven percent to 42, with support falling to 32.6 percent. 

 A member of the European Union since January 1995, Sweden decided not to join the euro at its launch in January 1999. 

 Analysts said memories of damaging exchange-rate fluctuations which surrounded Sweden's decision to abandon its peg to the Ecu, a precursor to the euro, in November 1992 are still engraved in dealers' minds. 

 But as long as the authorities give clear signals of their commitment to monetary and exchange stability, the jitters in the Swedish crown should be limited, analysts said. 

 "If the Danish referendum results in a 'No', of which there is a good chance, there is bound to be a pulic opinion effect in Sweden," said Darren Williams, economist at Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette in London. 

 "We could see some short-term negative market reaction in Denmark and we could see the same in Sweden, but as long as economic policy (in those countries) continue to be addressed towards stability I do not expect the reaction to go too far."

title: UPDATE 1-Danish  central bank  seen defending crown.
text:
COPENHAGEN, June 2 (Reuters) - Denmark's central bank intervened in the foreign exchange market on Friday, buying crowns against the euro in an effort to support the weakening currency, forex dealers said. 

 "They have been in this morning at 7.4640," one dealer told Reuters. 

 "They seem to be serious around forty (7.4640)," another dealer said, adding that the central bank had also been spotted acting through intermediaries in overseas markets. 

 Analysts said Denmark's central bank, whose chief monetary policy mandate is to maintain exchange rate stability rather than keeping inflation or money supply within set target ranges, seemed content to defend the crown through intervention rather than hiking interest rates. 

 "The central bank has masses of reserves so while they would defend the currency at all costs, I would be very surprised if they did anything on rates in the near future," said a currency trader at a Nordic bank in London. 

 The Danish central bank left key interest rates unchanged at Friday's regular weekly money market operation, offering to sell two-week certificates of deposit (CDs) and lend 14-day funds against collateral at unchanged rates of 4.10 percent. 

 Friday's intervention followed similar central bank action earlier in the week, traders said. 

 On Monday, the crown breached central parity of 7.46038 per euro for the first time. Analysts have attributed the currency's decline to opinion polls that show growing anti-euro sentiment. 

 Denmark will hold a referendum on joining the single currency on September 28. In the past fortnight, three opinion polls have put euro opponents ahead of supporters, denting the crown and resulting in wider yield spreads between Danish government bonds and euro zone benchmark Bunds. 

 At 0828 GMT, the crown was trading at 7.4635 against the euro, off an intra-day low of 7.4641. 

 The benchmark 10-year bond yield spread over Bunds was 54 basis points, up from 51 bps at Wednesday's close. Denmark's financial markets were closed on Thursday for the Ascension Day holiday. ((Peter Starck +45 33 96 96 50, fax +45 33 93 84 57, copenhagen.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Danish Ctrl Bk Seen Holding Rates Despite Weak Krone
text:
COPENHAGEN -(Dow Jones)- The Danish central bank is treading carefully ahead of a Sept. 28 vote on whether Denmark should join the euro, and will probably abstain from unilateral rate hikes to defend the krone, analysts say. 

 While the euro has nose-dived, the krone - which is linked to it - has been losing even more ground. 

 Monday the krone moved above its parity of DKK7.46038 compared with the euro, hitting its weakest level since the euro was launched in January 1999. 

 Since then, the Danish currency has improved slightly. At 1326 GMT Wednesday, it was trading at DKK7.4592. But it's still not far off lows, sparking market talk that the Danish central bank might be forced to use the interest rate weapon to support the krone. 

 Nevertheless, analysts say the central bank will only opt for rate hikes independently of the European Central Bank, if the krone approaches the bottom end of its trading band, and only if intervention doesn't succeed. 

 Under the terms of Denmark's currency agreement with the ECB, the krone can fluctuate up to 2.25% on each side of its parity. 

 Peter Schlaikjer Bruhn, analyst with LB Kiel Gudme Raaschou in Copenhagen noted that even in its present weakened state, the krone is still below its upper limit of DKK7.6282 against the euro. 

 Bruhn also said the central bank is particularly wary of getting embroiled in any political discussion on whether Denmark should join the euro, a subject of heated debate in the lead up to September's referendum. The upshot is that the bank is steering clear of acting in a way that may be perceived as politically partisan. 

 "The bank may be accused of taking a political stance if they move isolated on interest rates now," said Bo Overvad, analyst with Svenska Handelsbanken in Copenhagen. 

 Economists also note that Danish foreign reserves remain relatively high, so the central bank has ample ammunition to defend the currency if necessary. 

 April foreign reserves came in at DKK133.8 billion, down DKK5 billion from the previous month, but still higher than the total at the start of 1999. The May total isn't expected to decline significantly. 

 An unnamed analyst suggested that the central bank may even be content to see the krone at lower levels. "It's come close to its parity now and I think the bank is quite happy to see it staying around here in the period until the referendum in September," the anslyst said. 

 Many economists say that Denmark would like to enter the euro at parity if referendum voters agree to euro entry. 

 Denmark's sound economic fundamentals also minimize the likelihood of a rate hike. Economic forecasts released earlier Wednesday by the Danish Economic Council, predicted inflation will slow to an annual increase of 1.8% from 2.7% the previous year. At the same time exports are seen replacing private consumption as the main growth driver, alleviating price pressure. 

 "At this stage there is no reason to raise interest rates," said Svenska Handelsbanken's Overvad.

title: Danish c.bank seen selling euro to support crown.
text:
COPENHAGEN, Jan 21 (Reuters) - Denmark's central bank intervened in the foreign exchange market on Friday - selling euros for crowns - dealers said, dubbing the intervention undramatic. 

 One forex dealer said the bank was in the market for the second day running to shore up the crown, buying crowns for some 500 million euros on Friday alone. 

 The bank bought crowns for prices ranging between 7.4455 and 7.4460 crowns per euro, dealers said. 

 Last week the bank bought crowns for approximately 700-800 million euros, traders said. 

 A central bank official declined to comment, citing the bank's stated policy of not discussing its market operations in public. 

 Dealers said pressure on the crown did not stem from any speculation against Denmark, but from regular corporate sector interest. 

 Danish investors' needs to convert crowns into foreign currencies, amid ongoing portfolio diversification into overseas securities, was also bringing pressure to bear on the currency, dealers said. 

 The crown - which through most of 1999 traded in a range of 7.4325-7.4375 per euro - stood at 7.4455, slightly lower than late Thursday. 

 Since the euro's launch in January 1999, the Danish crown has consistently traded on the stronger side of its 7.46038 ERM-2 central parity.

title: Danish c.bank seen selling euro to shore up crown.
text:
COPENHAGEN, Jan 12 (Reuters) - Denmark's central bank intervened in the foreign exchange market on Wednesday - selling euros for crowns - dealers said, describing the intervention as undramatic. 

 One forex dealer said the bank was in the market for the third day running to shore up the crown while another market maker said small-scale intervention had been going on for about a week. 

 "We estimate that the central bank has bought Danish crowns for approximately 700 million euros in the past week," Nykredit Markets economist Steen Groendahl told Reuters. 

 A central bank official declined to comment, referring to the bank's stated policy of not discussing its market operations in public. 

 Dealers said the stability-oriented central bank was buying crowns to cushion a commercially driven weakening of the currency with the intention of preventing excessive intra-day swings versus the euro - its anchor in the ERM-2 grid. 

 The pressure on the crown was not stemming from any speculation against Denmark, but from regular corporate sector commercial interests strengthened by big Danish investors' needs to convert crowns into foreign currencies amid ongoing portfolio diversification into overseas securities, dealers said. 

 One dealer said short-term investment in the Danish crown had earlier offered a small yield pick-up over the euro zone, ensuring an inflow of foreign currency which tended to largely offset commercial outflows, keeping the crown-euro rate steady. 

 This yield pick-up virtually melted away recently, leaving the central bank as the only market player buying crowns, he said, speaking on condition of anonymity. 

 At 1205 GMT, an overnight investment in the euro yielded 3.02 percent against 3.05 percent for a same-maturity crown investment. 

 The crown - which through most of 1999 traded in a range of 7.4325-7.4375 per euro - stood at 7.4450, just off an intra-day low of 7.4453. 

 Since the euro's launch in January 1999, the Danish crown has consistently traded well on the stronger side of its 7.46038 ERM-2 central parity.

title: Danish crown 7.29252-7.62824 vs euro band - c.bank.
text:
COPENHAGEN, Dec 31 (Reuters) - Denmark's central bank said on Thursday the outer limits of the Danish crown's plus/minus 2.25 percent fluctuation band against the euro in the ERM-2 exchange rate mechanism will be 7.29252 and 7.62824. 

 Earlier, euro zone finance ministers, the European Central Bank (ECB) and Denmark and Greece agreed on an ERM-2 central parity exchange rate for the crown of 7.46038. Denmark and Greece are the starting members of ERM-2 - a grid for national currencies not taking part in the launch of the euro. 

 The Greek drachma's fluctuation band in ERM-2 is a wider plus/minus 15 percent. 

 "The intervention exchange rates are: sell rate 7.62824 crowns per euro, buy rate 7.29252," the Danish central bank said. 

 The ECB is obliged to help Denmark's central bank intervene in the foreign exchange market to keep the crown inside the agreed fluctuation range. Speculation may drive the Danish unit near the upper or lower limit of its ERM-2 band. 

 The Danish central bank has said its aim is to keep the crown within an unspecified narrower band than plus/minus 2.25 percent. 

 A foreign exchange trader at a Danish bank said he expected the crown would be kept in a range of 7.44-7.49 crowns per euro on a one-month horizon. 

 "Maybe in the longer term we will see a wider band," he said, referring to possible financial market volatility if forecasts of slower Danish economic growth materialised. 

 Between 1115 and 1345 GMT, commercial banks' indicative buy quotations for the crown against the euro ranged from 7.4207 to 7.4941.

title: Danish  central bank  says buys foreign  currency .
text:
COPENHAGEN, Sept 23 (Reuters) - Denmark's central bank said on Wednesday it intervened for the second consecutive day in the foreign exchange market, buying foreign currency for Danish crowns. 

 "We have been in the market. We bought foreign currency," central bank deputy director Kirsten Mordhorst said by telephone. She did not elaborate. 

 At 0920 GMT, the crown was at 3.8050 per German mark. It firmed to 3.8035 earlier in the session, the strongest level against the mark since December 3. 

 The crown appreciated sharply on Tuesday, with the DEM/DKK cross advancing to 3.8037 from 3.8128 at Monday's close. The central bank said on Tuesday afternoon it had sold crowns for foreign currencies to stabilise - in effect rein in the surge of - the Danish unit. 

 On Friday, the bank raised two key interest rates by one percentage point to 5.00 percent after four days of interventions to relieve pressure on the crown had failed. 

 Still on Monday, the bank had to intervene, selling foreign currencies to defend the crown, but on Tuesday the tide turned. 

 Financial daily Borsen on Wednesday quoted Den Danske Bank head of trading Mads Jacobsen as saying that the bank had once again demonstrated that it did not only talk about its stable crown exchange rate objective, but also meant it literally. 

 Exchange rate stability has been the cornerstone of Danish economic policy for 15 years, and Economy Minister Marianne Jelved said last week that the crown would be pegged to Europe's new euro currency within a narrow plus minus 2.25 percent fluctuation band. 

 An agreement on the band is expected to be announced after the September 25-27 meeting of European Union finance ministers and central bankers in Vienna. Analysts say such an agreement is likely to deter most speculators from going after the crown.

title: FOCUS-Surging crown sparks Danish cenbank action.
text:
COPENHAGEN, Sept 22 (Reuters) - Less than a week after it repeatedly intervened to support an ailing crown, Denmark's central bank was back in the market on Tuesday buying foreign currency to rein in a sharp rise in the currency. 

 The Danish crown appreciated strongly on Tuesday, hitting a 10-month high against the German mark and forcing the central bank's hand. The move marked a spectacular turnaround from last week's costly defence of the crown. 

 Having dug deep into its foreign exchange reserves to defend the crown last week, the bank on Friday raised two key interest rates by one percentage point to 5.00 percent, sparking a dramatic reversal in the crown. 

 Attracted by higher returns on crown-denominated instruments, funds began flowing actively into the market this week, said Jens Dalskov, an analyst at Den Danske Bank. 

 At 1500 GMT, the crown was at 3.8067 per mark compared with 3.8128 at Monday's close and last Friday's 3.8140 - the weakest level since May 7. 

 It hit 3.8037, the strongest since December 3, before the central bank's intervention nudged it into an afternoon band of 3.8040-3.8080. 

 "Our policy is to stabilise the crown," central bank deputy director Kirsten Mordhorst said by telephone. "We have been buying foreign currencies," she added. 

 Analysts noted that the Danish central bank was a regular operator in the foreign exchange market. Its stated objective is to ensure exchange rate stability, defined as a stable crown exchange rate against core European currencies, primarily the mark. This has succeeded for most of the past two years. 

 Unlike central banks in many other countries, the Danish monetary watchdog does not adjust interest rates to keep inflation in check. In Denmark, this is the responsibility of government fiscal policy. 

 Early in May, the bank raised key interest rates by half a percentage point to defend the crown after interventions in excess of 20 billion crowns ($3.1 billion) failed to end a run on the domestic currency. 

 The crown stabilised, and three weeks later, the bank shaved 25 basis points off its steering rates. 

 The crown remained static until late August, when a massive flight to quality sparked by the devaluation of the Russian rouble prompted foreign investors to dump holdings in peripheral markets, including Danish bonds. 

 On August 25-26, the central bank sold 15.7 billion crowns worth of foreign currencies to prevent the crown from weakening amid the sell-off. 

 At end-August, the bank's foreign exchange reserves stood at a 20-month low 90.9 billion crowns. It was unclear by how much the reserves were depleted during last week's support interventions. Analysts' estimates varied between 15 billion and 20 billion crowns. 

 The relatively low level of reserves made an immediate cut in key interest rates unlikely. 

 "They would probably like to see a rather considerable inflow (of foreign currencies) before they do anything," Dalskov said, adding he did not expect a move this week. 

 In Denmark, high short-term interest rates have only a minor effect on the real economy because most of household and corporate sector borrowing focus on long-term mortgage loans. 

 Thus an increase in short-term market rates does not raise a public outcry or prompt the political establishment to try to influence the central bank to moderate its policy, analysts say.
