title: Danish  central bank intervenes  after rates rise.
text:
COPENHAGEN, Sept 21 (Reuters) - Denmark's central bank said on Monday it intervened in the foreign exchange market to support the domestic crown currency. 

 On Friday, the central bank raised two key interest rates by one percentage point to 5.00 percent to defend the weakened crown after four days of interventions. 

 "We have been in the market, selling (foreign) currency," central bank deputy director Kirsten Mordhorst told Reuters by telephone on Monday. 

 At 0840 GMT, the crown traded at 3.8129 per German mark compared with 3.8118 after Friday's monetary tightening. Monday morning's lows against the mark was 3.8131. 

 "This is serious, and it is not over yet," one forex dealer said. Overseas investors were continuing to sell Danish bonds, triggering steady pressure on the crown. 

 The selling was not linked to particular Danish factors, but was a reflection of the uncertainty prevailing in global financial markets, prompting investors to flee peripheral markets for safe-haven paper in euroland, primarily German Bunds, dealers said. 

 Together with Scandinavian neighbour Sweden and Norway - the latter not a member of the European Union - Denmark will not join European economic and monetary union (EMU) at its scheduled January 1999 launch. 

 On Sunday, Danish Prime Minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen reiterated that a Danish referendum on EMU membership was not on the agenda within the next three to four years. Denmark cannot join EMU unless a majority of Danes vote in favour in a referendum. 

 The yield spread between Denmark's benchmark 7.00 percent 2007 state bond and 4.00 percent 2008 Bunds widened to 94 basis points from Friday's close at 76 basis points. 

 In the two-year maturity, the yield spread shot out to 171 basis points from 116.

title: ANALYSIS-Danish rates seen rising more to help DKK.
text:
COPENHAGEN, Sept 21 (Reuters) - The Danish crown came under renewed pressure on Monday and analysts said Friday's sharp increase in key interest rates may prove counter-productive, forcing the central bank to raise rates again to keep the crown steady. 

 For Denmark, the vexing characteristic of the present crown crisis was that it had not been caused by domestic factors. 

 The crown, stable against the German mark for most of the past 15 years, weakened amid a universal investor flight to safe-haven German and U.S. bonds, a trend accentuated in Denmark's case by its status as an EMU non-starter. 

 Analysts said the monetary tightening had actually served to alarm some investors who had been unaware of any trouble. 

 "It was definitely a bad move. Denmark implemented a major rate rise on the basis of a minor weakening of the crown," said Sharda Persaud, an economist with Paribas Bank in London. 

 "There is not a specific Danish reason for the run on the crown," said Georg Andersen, fixed income strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston (CSFB) in London. 

 "People want German Bunds. We are seeing some adjustments of foreign investors' holdings of Danish bonds across the board," he said. 

 Kai Lindberg, chief economist at Codan Bank, said flows indicated that Danish bonds had been sold for billions of crowns on Monday. 

 The slice of Danish bonds held by overseas investors could fall to around 35 percent from slightly over 40 percent before the turmoil started with the devaluation of the Russian rouble in mid-August, analysts said. 

 A stable crown exchange rate is a cornerstone of Danish economic policy, and analysts said the central bank would not hesitate to raise key interest rates more, if necessary, thus making investment in crown-denominated instruments more attractive, and borrowing in crown more expensive. 

 With most household and corporate sector borrowing in long-term mortgage loans, higher short-term market rates would not raise a public outcry or prompt the political establishment to influence the central bank to moderate its policy. 

 But some analysts said the central bank may have shot itself in the foot by Friday's aggressive one percentage point increase to 5.00 percent in two monetary steering tools, the repo and certificate of deposit rate. The tightening came at the end of the fourth consecutive day of intervention to support the crown. 

 "It will not take the pressure off the crown," CSFB's Andersen said. "They (the central bank) can stem the tide but they cannot avert the direction," he said. 

 "There is a perception that we could be in for more rate hikes," he added. 

 "If the pressure continues, and we suppose it will, they will have to raise rates again. The next move will be 200 basis points," said Lindberg at Codan Bank. 

 Persaud at Paribas said the next increase would have to be at least half a percentage point. 

 The central bank said on Monday it had again intervened in the foreign exchange market to support the crown. 

 The lack of a clear-cut result to Sunday's election in neighbouring Sweden also tended to be negative for the Danish crown, analysts said. 

 "We are seeing investors leaving the Scandinavian countries. They have left Norway already," Lindberg noted. 

 At 1115 GMT, the crown traded at 3.8129 per mark compared with 3.8118 after Friday's monetary tightening. Monday morning's lows against the mark was 3.8131 before the central bank intervened. 

 The yield spread between Denmark's benchmark 7.00 percent 2007 state bond and 4.00 percent 2008 Bunds widened to 111 basis points from Friday's close at 76 basis points. 

 In the two-year maturity, the yield spread shot out to 202 basis points from 116. 

 Denmark's inverted yield curve - two-month rates near 5.50 percent against 4.95 percent for 10-year paper - was regarded as a danger signal by some investors remembering that the same had occurred in Norway, Andersen said. 

 "We expect it (the curve) to stay inverse, even become more inverted next week or so," he said.

title: Danish  central bank intervenes  again to help crown.
text:
COPENHAGEN, Sept 17 (Reuters) - Denmark's central bank continued to intervene in the foreign exchange market on Thursday in an effort to relieve pressure on the crown. 

 "We have been in the market again," central bank deputy director Kirsten Mordhorst said. 

 Earlier, she said the bank had intervened in the morning as well, and confirmed that intervention was now going on for the third straight day. 

 In line with standard central bank policy, Mordhorst declined comment on intervention volumes or levels. 

 At 1335 GMT, the crown was at 3.8127 per mark. Forex dealers said the bank had bought crowns for mark at 3.8132 - the Danish unit's weakest level in four months. 

 The crown has softened gradually from 3.8080 on September 1. Central bank intervention to the amount of 15.7 billion crowns ($2.45 billion) on August 25-26 helped the currency strengthen from 3.8110 on August 26. 

 The latest bout of weakness set in on Tuesday after the release of a central bank quarterly report saying Denmark's 1998 current account could fall into deficit after eight years in surplus. 

 On Wednesday, the lowest bid level against the German unit was 3.8127, while the crown sank to 3.8130 on Tuesday when the central bank stepped in to support it, forex dealers said. 

 Dealers said Wednesday's intervention had been in the region of five billion crowns. 

 The central bank routinely acts in the foreign exchange market to keep the crown steady near its central parity rate against the mark in the EU Exchange Rate Mechanism.

title: Nordic  Forex : Danish Krone Down As Rate Rise Prospects Fade
text:
OSLO (Dow Jones)--The Danish krone (DKK) continued to lose ground against the Deutsche mark in late dealings Thursday, with fair selling interest overcoming intervention from Danmarks Nationalbank, the central bank of Denmark. 

 At 1437 GMT the mark was DKK3.8135, up from DKK3.8122 late Wednesday, and its strongest since it hit DKK3.8152 May 8 ahead of Denmark's referendum on the European Union's Amsterdam Treaty. 

 Dealers attributed some of the decline to fading expectations of a central bank interest rate rise to boost the currency. Most believe the central bank is more likely to continue on its present course of krone buying. 

 "A rate rise now would have led to heavier Danish bond sales and caused a further weakening of the krone," said the chief dealer with large Swedish bank. "It wouldn't have done any good in the near term," he added. 

 The Danish currency has been pressured recently by the weakening of the Norwegian and Swedish currencies and a flight from smaller European bond markets towards the safe haven of German bunds. 

 Market watchers greeted the surprise announcement Thursday that the krone will be linked to the euro by a narrow trading band of 2.25%, with enthusiasm, saying it should help restore long-term stability to the currency. 

 The deal is expected to be concluded at the EcoFin meeting of E.U. central bankers and finance ministers in Vienna later this month.

title: WSJE: Slide Continues For  Currencies  In Scandinavia
text:
From Thursday's Wall Street Journal Europe 


   By Almar Latour


 (Dow Jones)--Scandinavian currencies continued sliding against the U.S. dollar and mark, amid investor worries about the looming collapse of Russia's financial markets and a domino effect of the Asian crisis on emerging markets world-wide. 

 The currency crisis also sank its teeth into Scandinavia's political landscape, unleashing more political bickering over fiscal policy in Norway and forcing the issue of European economic and monetary union into Sweden's national election debate. 

 The Norwegian krone, marked by heavy losses against the mark in recent days, again depreciated the most among Scandinavian currencies, trading at 4.4410 kroner to the mark in late trading, compared with 4.3810 kroner on Tuesday and 4.0900 kroner in early January. The dollar rose to 8.3179 kroner from 8.2655 kroner on Tuesday. 

 The Swedish krona also dropped in value against the mark, although marginally. It traded at 4.6035 kronor against the mark compared with 4.6000 kronor on Tuesday and 4.2688 kronor in late April. The krona, however, had been sliding sharply against the mark all week. The dollar rose to 8.3179 kronor compared with 8.2655 kronor on Tuesday. 

 The Danish krone came under pressure as well and lost in trading against the dollar, as Denmark's central bank intervened to protect the currency's unofficial peg to the mark. The Danish krone traded at 6.8840 kroner against the U.S. dollar compared with 6.8590 kroner on Tuesday. The Danish krone remained firm against the mark, at its unofficial peg of about 3.8081 - but only after the Bank of Denmark intervened to support the Danish krone against the mark. 

 The depreciation of the Norwegian, Swedish and Danish currencies against the mark and dollar in recent days shows that currencies of countries outside the euro zone are more sensitive to external economic crises and investors' caprices than currencies that are members of EMU. 

 By contrast, the currency of EMU members are more solid. For example, Nordic neighbor Finland's currency - the markkaa - has proved to be the sole survivor recently in the local currency carnage. 

 "When there is turbulence, it's hard to stand alone," said Jonas Frycklund, EMU expert for the Federation of Swedish Industries. "That goes for both Sweden and Norway. Other countries simply enjoy more protection."

title: FX  CROSS-Mark/Drachma surges on Russia fears.
text:
LONDON, Aug 26 (Reuters) - The mark rose sharply against the drachma on Wednesday despite three interventions from the Bank of Greece as Russia fears took their toll. 

 Having fallen to a three-month low of 174.55, the drachma fought back after the third round of central bank support. 

 "Greece is considered the last emerging market in Europe and gets hit when ...things are tough," said Michael Lewis, currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London. 

 At 1500 GMT the drachma stood at 173.20/40 compared with 170.60/70 late Tuesday. 

 Elsewhere, the Norwegian and Swedish crowns extended recent losses against the mark due to Russia and a gloomy outlook for weaker commodity prices, analysts said. 

 But the mark slipped against the yen and dollar after German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said the G7 group of industrialised nations, International Monetary Fund and European Union cannot solve Russia's problems. 

 The mark fell to 80.00/02 yen, down from 80.56/59. 

 Analysts linked the peripheral currencies' tumble to a generalised move into core markets in light of Russia's difficulties. 

 "The problems in Russia and emerging market contagion effects are creating their own Scandinavian contagion," said David Brown, chief European economist at Bear Stearns in London. 

 The mark rose 1.9 percent against the Norwegian crown to 4.4595/6.25 against late Tuesday's 4.3770/90. 

Denmark's central bank said it intervened to prop up the crown against the German mark. The Danish crown was at session lows of 3.8080/83 against the mark, compared to Tuesday's late 3.8105/10. 

 "Our stated policy is to keep the crown steady," deputy director Kirsten Mordhorst, told Reuters. 

 Sweden followed Norway's lead at first, sinking to 4.6440/55 per mark against 4.5930/60 late on Tuesday. But the Swedish crown staged an afternoon rally to 4.6090/20 on rumours of Riksbank intervention. 

 But analysts said the pain may continue. 

 "I have no sense that these markets are out of woods yet," Bear Stearns' Brown said. "There will be no risk reversal on mark/Scandinavian crosses until we see recovery in Russia, which is far off." 

 He said the market is unlikely to differentiate between the Nordic currencies, despite Norway's higher dependence on oil. 

 But Kjell Tangen, general manager of Christiania Bank in London said he saw little reason for Norway's fall, much less Sweden's follow on. 

 "There is no reason from it apart from that they are small currencies outside the EMU area," he said. ((James Saft, London newsroom + 44 171 542 2734)).

title: DKK-euro band deal likely Sept-Oct-Danish minister.
text:
COPENHAGEN, Aug 26 (Reuters) - Danish Economy Minister Marianne Jelved said on Wednesday an agreement on the ERM-2 fluctuation band for the crown against the new euro currency was likely to be reached in September or October. 

 The prospects were good for a tight crown-euro band, Jelved told Reuters. Denmark and the European Central Bank are scheduled to start formal talks on the issue later this year. 

 ERM-2 will be a new exchange rate mechanism for national currencies of European Union countries not joining economic and monetary union (EMU) from the start in January 1999. 

 "There are good possibilities for Denmark to reach agreement on a narrow fluctuation band to the euro, and that this will happen in September," Jelved said. 

 "But it is also possible that the agreement will be reached only in October," she said. 

 Denmark would soon submit an official application to the European Union regarding an ERM-2 agreement, she said, but did not elaborate. 

 Denmark's decision on an exchange rate agreement would be made by the government, Jelved said. 

 Analysts expect a fluctuation band of +/-2.25 percent from the crown's central parity against the euro in ERM-2. 

 The central parity will be fixed at the end of this year when the 11 EU countries joining EMU merge their national currencies into the euro. 

 Both the ECB and Denmark's central bank are expected to be obliged to intervene in the foreign exchange market on behalf of the crown to keep it inside the agreed fluctuation range. 

 The cornerstone of Danish economic policy for the past 15 years has been to keep the crown exchange rate tightly linked to the German mark near its 3.8144 central parity in ERM. 

 Denmark will not join EMU in 1999 due to an opt-out from the single currency agreed as a condition for Danish approval of the EU's Maastricht Treaty in a 1993 referendum.

 The Finnish markka was slightly lower against the mark at 3.0400/30, against late Tuesday's 3.0379/0408. 

 Bear Stearns' Brown said the market is unlikely to differentiate between the Nordic currencies, despite Norway's higher dependence on oil prices. 

 But Kjell Tangen, general manager of Christiania Bank London said he saw little reason for Norway's fall, much less Sweden's follow on. 

 "There is no reason from it apart from that they are small currencies outside the EMU area," he said. "I would reckon this is just a temporary situation." 

 The Greek drachma was also pulled into Russia's vortex, falling against the mark and prompting intervention from the Bank of Greece. 

 The drachma was at 171.65/85 against the mark, down from 170.60/70 in late Tuesday trade but above an earlier three-month low at 171.95. 

 Greece's decision on Tuesday to pull the privatisation of Ionian Bank has also dented sentiment towards the drachma.

title: Denmark has target for crown-euro fluctuation band.
text:
COPENHAGEN, May 29 (Reuters) - Denmark has set its own target for the width of the fluctuation band for the crown currency in Europe's future exchange rate mechanism, ERM-2, Prime Minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen said on Friday. 

 His government is aiming for a narrower band than +/-15 percent from central parity exchange rates, he told a news conference, but declined to be more specific. 

 "We have ideas what we would like to have. We know that the financial markets have ideas, too, and we will meet some day," he said. 

 Denmark would be in shape to join European economic and monetary union, but its opt-out from the single currency - negotiated in 1992 and approved by the Danes in a 1993 referendum - means that the crown will be pegged to the new euro inside ERM-2 from January 1, 1999. 

 Rasmussen said fluctuation limits of +/-15 percent were for "everybody." 

 "I would prefer a more slim variation channel...and I hope there will be an understanding saying that we could have perhaps a smaller degree of variation," he said. 

 "I cannot give any concrete figure right now," he said, noting that the band would be negotiated between his country and the eleven EMU starters - all EU members except the UK, Sweden, Greece and Denmark. 

 "Economy Minister Marianne Jelved will be engaged in obtaining the best possible agreement," Rasmussen said. 

 No decisions have been made, but Denmark is aiming for a deal that would include intervention on behalf of the crown by the coming European Central Bank, should the crown come under pressure. 

 "We think that we could pursue a good agreement of mutual support, because I hope that the others will realise that we have a strong and sound economy," Rasmussen said, adding Denmark was expecting good co-operation on monetary issues with the euro-11. 

 He reiterated that a referendum on scrapping the single currency opt-out would not be held any time soon. 

 "Let us see the baby grow in the coming years, see how it is functioning. Let us take good time to evaluate things. Nobody should be stressed," he said. 

 "In or out of EMU, the Danes and the country will anyhow need to pursue a strong and responsible economic policy. That is the basic issue," the premier said. 

 ((Peter Starck +45 33 96 96 50 fax +45 33 93 84 57, copenhagen.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Nordic  Forex : Danish Krone Steady, But Still Shaky Early
text:
COPENHAGEN (Dow Jones)--The Danish krone (DKK) is steady, but shaky Thursday morning after a strong foreign sell-off Wednesday forced Denmark's central bank to intervene to prop up the currency. 

 At 0855 GMT, the Deutsche mark fetched DKK3.8140, higher than DKK3.8157 late Wednesday. So far, volume is thin, with attention instead focused on the short-end of the money market. Dealers expect the krone to trade from DKK3.8140 to DKK3.8150 Thursday. 

 In recent weeks, the krone has slowly weakened amid growing concern over the Danish referendum May 28 to ratify the Amsterdam Treaty, which prepares for European Union expansion. Investors fear that a rejection of the treaty by the E.U.-skeptic Danes could jeopardize the country's future relationship in the E.U. 

 In recent days, the central bank has been forced to spend DKK3 to DKK4 billion a session to support the currency, some dealers say. According to the latest round of foreign currency reserve figures, the central bank spent DKK16 billion in support of the krone in April. 

 The bank's decision Tuesday to raise its discount and securities repurchase interest rates, by 0.5% to 4.0% and 4.25% respectively, has done little to stem selling of the currency, dealers added. This is sparking speculation the bank will be forced to raise rates again soon. 

 'There has been an uncertainty due to the Amsterdam Treaty referendum in May,' said one dealer in Copenhagen. 'If we see a further weakening, the central bank could take action with interest rates again. But it's not in the picture at the moment.' 

 The krone slipped as far as DKK3.8160 per mark in late trade Wednesday, weakening from DKK3.8155 before the rate increase and well above its level of DKK3.8133 before the start of Denmark's 11-day nationwide strike.

title: Danish  central bank  buys crowns for marks - dealers.
text:
COPENHAGEN, May 6 (Reuters) - Denmark's central bank intervened in the foreign exchange market on Wednesday afternoon, buying crowns at 3.8154 per mark, forex dealers said. 

 "The central bank has bought crowns for marks at 3.8154," one dealer said. 

 The central bank declined comment, having said earlier in the day that it had not been in the market on Wednesday. 

 At 1400, the crown traded at 3.8151 per mark compared with 3.8137 at Tuesday's close. 

 On Tuesday, the central bank raised key interest rates by 50 basis points to defend the crown. It said it had been buying crowns since February, and that the foreign currency outflow, which increased in April had continued in early May. 

 Dealers earlier said the crown was weakening with foreign investors selling amid concern over Denmark's May 28 referendum on the European Union's Amsterdam Treaty.

title: EMS Focus: Denmark Krone Steady Despite Election Rumors
text:
COPENHAGEN (AP-Dow Jones)--The Danish krone is expected to remain steady as a rock in the days ahead, in part due to an absence of concern among investors about the possibility of a snap general election being called for next month, analysts said. 

 Also, the persistent steadiness of the Danish currency is a testament to the successful intervention of Denmark's central bank, which uses monetary policy solely to ensure a steady exchange rate versus the Deutsche mark. 

 Analysts argue that the only event which could really rock the krone is an unexpected rejection of the European Union's Amsterdam Treaty when a referendum is held on it next spring. 

 'There is such huge credibility in the market today towards the central bank's exchange rate policy,' said Jakob Vejlo, chief economist with Unibank Markets in Copenhagen. 'But if we say `No' to the Amsterdam Treaty, we will probably run into some volatility with the currency.' 

 At 1115 GMT Wednesday, the Deutsche mark fetched 3.8072 kroner, compared with 3.8079 at the close of European trading Tuesday. Denmark's ERM central parity rate is 3.81443 kroner to the mark. 

 In April or May, Denmark will hold a referendum on the Amsterdam Treaty, which is designed to prepare the 15-nation bloc for expansion. From a legal point of view, rejection of the treaty, which was agreed in June, could nullify the document and even raise questions about Denmark's future participation in the union.
